parts.label: a
parts.text:
You recently took part in a cooking competition at your school.

Write an email to a friend about the competition.

In your email:
• Explain why you decided to enter the competition.
• Describe what you cooked and how you prepared it.
• Say what you learned from the experience.

Write about 120 to 160 words. You will receive up to 6 marks for the content of your email, and up to 9 marks for the style and accuracy of your language.
parts.answer: Model answer (one of many acceptable): Hi Ali, Guess what? Last Friday I entered the school cooking competition! I only signed up because my mum said my chicken karahi was better than hers, and I wanted to see if the judges agreed. We had just forty-five minutes to cook. I chopped onions, tomatoes and green chillies as fast as I could, then fried the chicken with ginger and garlic. Halfway through I realised I'd forgotten the salt, so I was really nervous when the judges tasted it! In the end I came third, which I'm proud of. The biggest lesson was that planning matters: if I'd written a list of steps, I wouldn't have panicked. Next year I'm going to practise with a timer. Why don't you enter with me? Write soon, Hamza

parts.answer: Model answer (one of many acceptable): Dear Sana, I'm sorry I haven't written for ages — I've been so busy with my cousin Ayesha's wedding! It took place in a big marquee in my uncle's garden in Sialkot. My favourite part was the mehndi night. All the girls had henna on their hands, and we sang old songs while my aunts played the dholak. I laughed so much my face hurt! Then, on the main day, something surprising happened: just as the bride arrived, the electricity went off. For a few minutes everyone stood in the dark, but then my younger brother switched on the generator and the guests cheered as if he were the hero of the day. The photographs by candlelight actually look beautiful. I'll show you when I see you next week. Love, Mahnoor

parts.answer: Model answer (one of many acceptable): Hi Zara, You'll never guess where I spent Saturday — at an animal shelter! My neighbour volunteers there and she said they needed extra help because so many puppies had been brought in. I started by cleaning out the cages, which wasn't very pleasant, I must admit. After that I mixed food for the cats and filled about thirty water bowls. The best part was taking two of the older dogs for a walk in the park next door; one of them, a brown dog called Sheru, kept trying to lick my face! By the end I was exhausted but happy. I definitely want to go back next month. It felt good to do something useful, and I'd love to see if Sheru finds a family. Maybe you could come too? Best wishes, Omar

parts.answer: Model answer (one of many acceptable): Hi Bilal, How are you? Last Tuesday our class visited a sports-goods factory in Sialkot for our business studies project. We're learning how products are made and sold abroad. The most interesting thing was watching workers stitch footballs by hand. One man told us he could finish a ball in under two hours, and every stitch looked perfect. We also saw machines that test how well the balls bounce, which was surprisingly fun. To be honest, I'm not sure I'd like to work there. The factory was very noisy and hot, and doing the same task all day would bore me. However, I'd love to work in the export office, because they talk to customers from all over the world. Let me know how your exams went! Ahmed

I ran in the 4 × 100 metre relay with three girls from my class. I was the last runner, so everyone was depending on me. For three weeks before the race we practised passing the baton every morning before school, because our PE teacher said that's where most teams lose time. On the day, we were in second place when I got the baton, and I managed to overtake the girl in front just before the line! At the end of the day I felt tired but incredibly proud, especially when my little brother ran to hug me. I hope your sports day goes well too. Lots of love, Amna

parts.answer: Model answer (one of many acceptable): Hi Faisal, I've just got back from a family trip to the beach at Gaddani, and I wanted to tell you about it. I went with my parents, my two sisters and my grandfather, who hadn't seen the sea for twenty years. We left Karachi early to avoid the heat. At the beach, my sisters and I collected shells while my father set up a big umbrella. Later we had a camel ride along the shore, which was bumpy but hilarious. The best moment was at sunset, when my grandfather sat on the sand and started telling us stories about fishing with his father when he was a boy. I'd never heard those stories before, and it made the day really special. We should go together next time! Your friend, Danish

parts.answer: Model answer (one of many acceptable): Hi Mehreen, You will never guess what happened! Last month our school choir performed at the city music festival, and I was picked to sing the solo in the final song. I had joined the choir in Year 8 because my sister was already a member, but I only got the solo after our music teacher heard me singing in the corridor. On the day, the hall was packed and the stage lights were so bright that I could hardly see the audience. My voice shook during the first verse, and my music sheet nearly slipped out of my hands. However, I took a deep breath, looked at our conductor, and the rest of the song went smoothly. Looking back, I learned that nerves are normal and that preparation matters more than perfection. The audience gave us a standing ovation, and I still cannot believe it! Are you coming to the concert next term? Let me know soon, Zoya

parts.answer: Model answer (one of many acceptable): Dear Mariam, I have to tell you about the scariest thing I've ever done! Our head teacher asked me to speak at assembly about the environment club, because I'd organised the tree-planting week. Five hundred students, plus all the teachers! The night before, I could hardly sleep, and in the morning my hands were shaking so much that my notes rustled into the microphone. Once I started, though, something surprising happened: when I mentioned that we'd planted 200 trees, people clapped, and suddenly I felt calm. I even made a joke that got a laugh. Looking back, I spoke much too fast at the beginning. Next time, I'll practise in front of my family first and remember to breathe between sentences. Have you ever had to do something like this? Write back soon! Noor

There are people of all ages, from teenagers to a retired doctor who's faster than all of us. I decided to join because I'd been spending far too long on my phone, and my cousin, who's a member, kept telling me how great it was. It has changed my life more than I expected. I go to bed earlier on Saturdays so that I'm fresh for the ride, and I've started cycling to school too, which saves my parents petrol money. I also feel much fitter. You should borrow your brother's bike and come with us one week! Cheers, Usman

parts.answer: Model answer (one of many acceptable): Dear Areeba, Remember I told you we were planning something for flood relief? Well, last Saturday our class held a charity food fair at school! The money went to families in Sindh who lost their homes. Organising it was harder than I thought. Two days before, the company that was supposed to lend us tables cancelled. I panicked, but then our science teacher suggested borrowing desks from the classrooms, and the caretaker helped us carry them out. On the day, the playground was packed. My samosas sold out in an hour, and a parent bought every single cake on one stall! Altogether we raised 85,000 rupees, which was more than double our target. I felt exhausted but really proud. I'll send you some photos tonight. Love, Kiran

parts.answer: Model answer (one of many acceptable): Hi Sara, At last I've been to Lahore Fort! Ever since my history teacher showed us pictures of the Sheesh Mahal, I'd dreamed of seeing it for myself. My uncle took me last weekend. We walked through the huge Alamgiri Gate, then spent ages in the Hall of Mirrors. When the guide lit a small candle, thousands of tiny pieces of glass on the ceiling sparkled like stars. Afterwards we climbed onto the walls and looked across at the Badshahi Mosque. Honestly, it was even better than I'd imagined. Photographs can't show how enormous everything is, or how cool and quiet it feels inside the thick walls. The only disappointment was that some areas were closed for repairs, so I'll have to go back. Shall we go together in the holidays? Hassan

The younger boy couldn't believe how spicy our food was and drank about ten glasses of lassi a day. I learned a lot from them. Our school organised a 'Switch-Off Saturday' because a survey showed most of us spend more than six hours a day on screens. I honestly thought I'd go crazy. In the morning I kept reaching for my phone, out of habit. To keep busy, I helped my grandmother in the kitchen, and she taught me how to make proper round rotis — mine looked like maps! In the afternoon I played cricket in the street with the neighbours' kids, and in the evening I read half a novel I'd bought months ago. Afterwards I felt surprisingly relaxed, and I slept really well. I'm not giving up my phone forever, but I'm going to try one screen-free evening a week. Try it! Talha

parts.answer: Model answer (one of many acceptable): Dear Hamid, I've just finished a four-week first-aid course run by the Red Crescent, and I thought you'd be interested. I chose it after my little brother fell off his bicycle last year and none of us knew what to do — it was a horrible feeling of helplessness. The hardest part was learning CPR. You have to press on the chest of a dummy far harder and faster than you'd expect, and after two minutes my arms were burning. At first I was embarrassed to keep getting the rhythm wrong, but the trainer suggested counting along to a song in my head, and that really worked. Now I feel far more confident. I'm hoping to volunteer at sports events, and one day I might even study nursing. Who knows, I could save a life! Take care, Rabia

parts.answer: Model answer (one of many acceptable): Hi Sobia, You've probably noticed that Laiba and I weren't speaking last week. It all started with a silly misunderstanding. She saw a photo of me at a café with some girls from another class and thought I'd gone without her on purpose, even though she'd told me she was busy that day. Instead of asking me, she just stopped replying to my messages. I was hurt and, honestly, quite angry, because I felt I'd done nothing wrong. At the same time I missed her terribly — lunch breaks were so boring! In the end I went round to her house and we talked for two hours. We both apologised and laughed about how stubborn we'd been. I've learned that it's always better to talk face to face than to guess what someone is thinking. Love, Maira

• Describe the lorries and the damage they are causing.
• Explain how the situation has affected the residents' daily lives.
• Suggest what the authorities could do and what the residents could do together.

parts.answer: Model answer (one of many acceptable): Hi Mr Qureshi, I hope you are well. Since the new ring road opened, lorries have been using our street as a shortcut, and they are far too heavy for it. Every time one passes, the windows rattle and the cups in the cabinet jump. There are cracks in the pavement near the corner, and the small shop has had its shutters damaged twice. My son can't sleep at night, and my husband is worried that the walls will crack. The council should put a weight limit on our street and install speed bumps. Residents could also record the number of lorries each day and send the figures to the council as evidence. Warmly, Rubab

practice.stem:
Read the article about a teenager who keeps bees in northern Pakistan, and then answer the questions.

The bee boy of the valley
When Bilal Khan was twelve, his grandfather gave him a wooden box with a small colony of bees inside. 'He told me that if I looked after them for one summer, I could keep any honey they made,' Bilal remembers. Five years later, the seventeen-year-old looks after forty hives on the hillside behind his family's house in Swat.
At first, Bilal was stung almost every day. He soon learned that bees become nervous when people move quickly, so he now works slowly and calmly. He also checks the hives early in the morning, when most of the bees are still inside and the air is cool.
The hardest time of year is winter. Snow covers the valley and there are no flowers, so Bilal feeds his colonies with sugar syrup until spring. In March, the apple and apricot trees begin to blossom and the bees become busy again.
Bilal sells most of his honey at the Saturday market in Mingora, where customers pay more for honey from bees that have fed on wild herbs. He has used the money to buy a second-hand motorbike, which he uses to carry hives to new places when the flowers near his home are finished.
His biggest ambition is to study agriculture at university. 'People think beekeeping is just about honey,' he says, 'but without bees, the farmers here would have far fewer apples.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: How old was Bilal when he was given his first bees?
parts.working: Accept 12. Do not accept 17.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Who gave Bilal the bees?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Why does Bilal now work slowly with the bees?
parts.answer: bees become nervous when people move quickly
parts.working: Accept 'so the bees don't get nervous'. Do not accept 'to avoid being stung' alone.

parts.label: d
parts.text: What does Bilal feed the bees in winter?
parts.working: Accept 'syrup'. Do not accept 'sugar' alone.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Where does Bilal sell most of his honey?
parts.working: Accept 'Saturday market'.

parts.label: f
parts.text: What does Bilal use his motorbike for?
parts.answer: to carry / move hives to new places (when nearby flowers are finished)
parts.working: Do not accept 'to go to the market'.

Books on wheels
Every Tuesday morning, a bright green bus parks outside the girls' school in Saryab Road, Quetta, and within minutes a queue of excited children forms at its door. The bus is not taking anyone anywhere. Inside, its seats have been replaced by shelves holding more than 2,000 books in Urdu, English, Pashto and Balochi.
The mobile library was started three years ago by a retired teacher, Mrs Nasreen Baloch. 'Many schools in the city have no library at all,' she explains. 'I couldn't build twenty libraries, but I could bring one library to twenty schools.'
The bus was bought with money from a local business owner, and volunteers painted it themselves over two weekends. Its route now includes eighteen schools and two parks, and it stops at each place once a week.
Children can borrow two books at a time. Mrs Baloch was worried at first that many books would never come back, but she says fewer than five a month are lost. The most popular books are adventure stories, followed closely by books about animals.
In winter, when temperatures in Quetta can fall well below zero, the bus has a small heater so that children can sit and read inside. Next year, Mrs Baloch hopes to add a second bus that will visit villages outside the city.

practice.stem:
Read the article about night-sky tours in the Cholistan Desert, and then answer the questions.

Stargazing in the desert
Most visitors to the Cholistan Desert come to see Derawar Fort, which rises from the sand like a huge brown ship. But a small tour company in Bahawalpur is now encouraging people to stay after dark.
'In big cities like Lahore, light from streets and buildings hides most of the stars,' says guide Usman Tariq. 'Here, on a clear night, you can see thousands of them with your own eyes.'
The tours leave Bahawalpur at four in the afternoon so that guests arrive before sunset. After a simple dinner of daal and roti cooked over a fire, Usman sets up two telescopes on a low sand dune. The best months for stargazing are October to March, when the air is dry and the nights are cool. In summer, dust in the air often makes the sky hazy.
Usman first became interested in astronomy at the age of nine, when his father pointed out the planet Jupiter to him. He has no formal training, but he has read dozens of books and taught himself to use the telescopes by watching videos online.
Guests are asked to bring warm clothes, because the desert becomes surprisingly cold at night, even after a hot day. They are also asked not to use their phone screens during the tour, as even a small light makes it harder for everyone's eyes to adjust to the darkness.

parts.working: Accept 'light pollution' / 'city lights'.

parts.text: At what time do the tours leave Bahawalpur?

parts.text: Why is summer not a good time for stargazing?

parts.working: Do not accept 'reading books' alone.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Why are guests asked not to use their phone screens?

Read the article about an old cinema in Hyderabad, Sindh, and then answer the questions.

A second life for the Palace Cinema
For almost twenty years, the Palace Cinema in Hyderabad stood empty. Its windows were broken, pigeons nested in the projection room and the famous painted sign above the entrance had faded until nobody could read it. Now, thanks to a group of young architects, the building has opened its doors again.
The project was led by Sana Memon, who used to watch films there with her grandmother as a child. 'I remember the smell of roasted peanuts and the sound of the audience cheering for the hero,' she says. 'I couldn't let the building be knocked down.'
The restoration took two and a half years. The biggest problem was the roof, which had let in rainwater for many years and damaged the wooden floor underneath. The team saved the original seats, which were sent to a workshop in Karachi to be repaired and re-covered in red cloth.
Today the Palace is more than a cinema. During the day it is used as a space for art exhibitions and music lessons, and on Friday evenings it shows old classic films for a ticket price of just 200 rupees.
The cinema's new sign was painted by hand by a 70-year-old artist who had created film posters for the Palace in the 1970s.

practice.stem:
Read the article about volunteers who protect sea turtles near Karachi, and then answer the questions.

Night shift on the beach
Between August and December, Hina Shah spends three nights every week walking along a dark beach west of Karachi with a torch covered in red plastic. She is one of about thirty volunteers who help to protect green turtles, which come ashore here to lay their eggs.
'The red light is important,' Hina explains. 'Bright white light confuses the turtles, but they hardly notice red.'
A female turtle digs a hole in the sand with her back flippers and lays around 100 eggs before covering them up and returning to the sea. The volunteers then mark the nest with a small wooden stick so that people do not walk on it. If a nest is too close to the water, they move the eggs carefully to a fenced area higher up the beach.
About seven weeks later, the baby turtles hatch and race towards the waves. The greatest danger they face on the beach is from wild dogs and crows. Further out, plastic bags floating in the sea are a serious threat, because turtles mistake them for jellyfish.
Hina, who studies marine biology, first joined the project after a school trip in Year 9. She says the most exciting moment of her life was watching 120 hatchlings reach the sea on a single night.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many nights a week does Hina work on the beach?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why does Hina use red light instead of white light?
parts.answer: white light confuses the turtles (but they hardly notice red)

parts.label: c
parts.text: What does a turtle use to dig its nest?
parts.working: Do not accept 'flippers' if 'front' is added.

parts.label: d
parts.text: What do the volunteers use to mark a nest?

parts.label: e
parts.text: What is the greatest danger to baby turtles on the beach?
parts.working: Both needed. Do not accept 'plastic bags' (danger in the sea).

parts.label: f
parts.text: When did Hina first join the project?
parts.answer: after a school trip in Year 9

practice.stem:
Read the article about a teenage chess coach in Nigeria, and then answer the questions.

The youngest coach in the club
On Saturday afternoons, the hall of a community centre in Lagos fills with the quiet click of chess pieces. At the front of the room, fifteen-year-old Tunde Adebayo moves between the tables, giving advice to players of all ages, including some who are old enough to be his grandparents.
Tunde learned chess from a library book when he was eight, practising alone with pieces made from bottle tops. His older cousin noticed his talent and took him to a local club, where he won his first tournament a year later.
Two years ago, the club's coach moved to another city, and nobody wanted to take his place. Tunde volunteered. 'I was nervous at first, because I'm younger than most of the members,' he says. 'But chess doesn't care how old you are.'
The club now has sixty members, more than double the number it had before Tunde became coach. He believes the secret is his rule that every lesson ends with a game against a partner of a different age.
Tunde's dream is to become an international master. For now, he is saving money from teaching private lessons so that he can travel to a tournament in Ghana next year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Where does Tunde coach chess?
parts.answer: (the hall of) a community centre in Lagos

parts.label: b
parts.text: How did Tunde first learn to play chess?
parts.working: Do not accept 'from his cousin'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What were Tunde's first chess pieces made from?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Why did the club need a new coach?
parts.answer: the (old) coach moved to another city

parts.label: e
parts.text: How many members does the club have now?

parts.label: f
parts.text: Why is Tunde saving money?
parts.answer: to travel to a tournament in Ghana (next year)
parts.working: Accept 'to go to a tournament in Ghana'.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a school farmers' market in Faisalabad, and then answer the questions.

Market day at school
Every Thursday afternoon, the playground of a girls' secondary school in Faisalabad turns into a small market. Tables are set up under the neem trees, and students sell vegetables that they have grown in the school's own garden.
The idea came from Mrs Nasreen Akram, who teaches biology. 'I wanted students to see where food really comes from,' she explains. 'Most of them had never planted a seed.' The garden was started three years ago on a piece of empty land behind the science block.
Students in Grades 8 and 9 look after the garden during their lunch break. They grow spinach, tomatoes, coriander and chillies in winter, and okra and gourds in the hot months. Water comes from a tank that collects rain from the school roof.
Parents are the market's best customers. Prices are lower than in the city bazaar, and the vegetables are picked only an hour before the market opens.
The money is not spent on the garden. Instead, it pays the school fees of two students whose families cannot afford them. 'That makes every bunch of coriander feel important,' says Hira, aged fourteen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: On which day of the week is the market held?

parts.label: b
parts.text: What subject does Mrs Akram teach?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Where in the school was the garden started?
parts.answer: (on empty land) behind the science block
parts.working: Do not accept 'the playground' (where the market is held).

parts.label: d
parts.text: When do students work in the garden?

parts.label: e
parts.text: Where does the water for the garden come from?
parts.answer: a tank that collects rain(water) from the school roof
parts.working: Accept 'rainwater from the roof'. 'A tank' alone is not enough.

parts.label: f
parts.text: What is the money from the market used for?
parts.answer: (paying) the school fees of two students (whose families cannot afford them)
parts.working: Do not accept 'the garden'.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a teenager who repairs old bicycles in Peshawar, and then answer the questions.

Second life for old bikes
In a narrow lane in Peshawar's old city, sixteen-year-old Aimal Khan spends most evenings surrounded by wheels, chains and tins of paint. He collects bicycles that people have thrown away and makes them ride like new.
Aimal learned the basics from his uncle, who has owned a cycle shop for thirty years. 'At first I was only allowed to pump up tyres,' he laughs. 'It took a whole year before he let me touch a gear.'
Most of the bicycles come from families who have bought motorbikes and no longer need them. Aimal pays nothing for them; he simply offers to take them away. The most difficult part of the job is removing rust, which can take a full day for a single frame.
He has repaired fifty-three bicycles so far. Instead of selling them, he gives them to students in nearby villages who live more than three kilometres from their school. 'A bike can save a child two hours of walking every day,' he says.
Aimal's next plan is to teach a group of girls from his neighbourhood how to fix punctures, so that they can look after their own bicycles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How old is Aimal?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Who taught Aimal how to repair bicycles?

parts.label: c
parts.text: What was the first job Aimal was allowed to do?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Why do many families no longer need their bicycles?

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which part of the job does Aimal find most difficult?
parts.working: Do not accept 'repairing gears'.

parts.label: f
parts.text: How many bicycles has Aimal repaired so far?

practice.stem:
Read the article about a community radio station in Tharparkar, and then answer the questions.

The voice of the desert
In a small village in Tharparkar, a single room built of mud bricks is home to a radio station that reaches more than forty villages. Its signal travels about twenty-five kilometres across the sand dunes.
The station was set up six years ago by a group of local teachers. They wanted to share useful information with families who do not have televisions or regular newspapers. Today it broadcasts for five hours every evening, from six until eleven.
The most popular programme is a weather report for farmers and herders, read in the local language, Dhatki. Listeners also enjoy a phone-in show on Fridays when people request folk songs for their relatives.
All the presenters are volunteers. Seventeen-year-old Kavita reads the children's news on Mondays. 'Before, I was too shy to speak in class,' she says. 'Now hundreds of people hear my voice every week.'
The station's electricity comes from four solar panels on the roof. During long cloudy periods in the monsoon, the team uses a small battery to stay on air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How far does the station's signal travel?
parts.working: Do not accept 'forty villages'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Who started the radio station?

parts.label: c
parts.text: At what time does the station stop broadcasting each evening?

parts.label: d
parts.text: In which language is the weather report read?

parts.label: e
parts.text: What does Kavita present?

parts.label: f
parts.text: What does the station use during cloudy periods in the monsoon?
parts.working: Do not accept 'solar panels'.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a floating market in Thailand, and then answer the questions.

Shopping by boat
Long before supermarkets arrived, many villages in central Thailand were connected only by canals, and people bought and sold food from small wooden boats. A few of these floating markets still exist today.
At one market, about two hours' drive from Bangkok, trading begins at seven in the morning and is mostly finished by noon. Sellers paddle slowly along the canal, calling out to customers who stand on wooden platforms at the water's edge.
Mrs Somchai, aged sixty-eight, has sold coconut pancakes from her boat for more than forty years. She cooks them on a small charcoal stove at the front of the boat. 'My mother sold the same pancakes from the same boat,' she says proudly.
Tourists now make up more than half of the customers, and some sellers have started offering souvenirs instead of fruit. Mrs Somchai is not worried by the change. 'Visitors still want to eat,' she smiles.
The local council has recently banned motorboats in the market area during trading hours. Engine noise was frightening customers, and the waves were damaging the old wooden houses beside the canal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How were many villages in central Thailand connected in the past?

parts.label: b
parts.text: At what time does trading begin?
parts.working: Do not accept 'noon'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Where do customers stand?
parts.answer: on wooden platforms at the water's edge

parts.label: d
parts.text: What does Mrs Somchai cook her pancakes on?

parts.label: e
parts.text: What have some sellers started selling instead of fruit?

parts.label: f
parts.text: Give ONE reason why motorboats were banned in the market area.
parts.answer: engine noise frightened customers / waves damaged the (old wooden) houses
parts.working: Either point for 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a business that makes paper from banana plants in Uganda, and then answer the questions.

Paper from the plantation
Once a banana plant has produced its fruit, the farmer cuts it down, because each stem fruits only once. In most of Uganda, these thick stems are simply left to rot in the fields. Grace Namutebi saw them differently.
'I was looking at a pile of old stems on my uncle's farm and I noticed how strong the fibres were,' she says. 'I wondered whether they could replace the wood that is normally used for paper.'
It took Grace almost a year of experiments in her kitchen to find the right method. The stems are first cut into strips and boiled for several hours to soften them. The fibres are then beaten into a pulp, spread thinly on screens and left to dry in the sun. The finished sheets are slightly rough and pale yellow in colour.
Grace's company now employs twenty-five people, most of them women from nearby villages. Farmers who sell their used stems to the company earn a small extra income from something they once threw away.
At first, Grace sold notebooks and greeting cards to tourists. However, her biggest customers today are hotels, which buy the paper for menus and packaging. Grace says the most difficult part of the business is not making the paper but persuading people that it is just as good as ordinary paper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Why do farmers cut down a banana plant after it has produced fruit?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Where did Grace first get the idea for her paper?
parts.working: Accept 'looking at old stems on her uncle's farm'. Do not accept 'in her kitchen'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What is done to the strips of stem to soften them?
parts.answer: they are boiled for several hours

parts.label: d
parts.text: What colour is the finished paper?

parts.label: e
parts.text: Who are Grace's biggest customers today?
parts.working: Do not accept 'tourists' (earlier customers).

parts.label: f
parts.text: According to Grace, what is the most difficult part of the business?
parts.answer: persuading people that the paper is as good as ordinary paper
parts.working: Do not accept 'making the paper'.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a cycling school for adults in Lahore, and then answer the questions.

Never too old to ride
Rukhsana Bibi was fifty-two when she sat on a bicycle for the first time. 'My brothers all had bikes when we were children, but girls in our street were not allowed,' she says. 'I always felt I had missed something.'
Last spring she joined a cycling school in a quiet park in Lahore that teaches adults – most of them women – how to ride. The school was set up by Ayesha Malik, an engineer who cycles to work every day. She started it after colleagues kept asking how she had learned.
Lessons take place early on Sunday mornings, before the park becomes crowded. Beginners start on bicycles with the pedals removed, pushing themselves along with their feet until they can balance. Only then are the pedals put back on. Most learners can ride on their own after four or five lessons, although a few need more time.
The bicycles are borrowed from a local repair shop, whose owner lends them free of charge. Learners pay a small fee, which is used to buy helmets.
Rukhsana now rides to the market twice a week instead of taking a rickshaw. She says she has saved money, but the biggest change is that she feels more independent. Her next goal is to teach her granddaughter to ride.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Why did Rukhsana not ride a bicycle as a child?
parts.answer: girls in her street were not allowed (to ride)

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is Ayesha Malik's job?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Why are lessons held early on Sunday mornings?

parts.label: d
parts.text: What do beginners do before the pedals are put back on?
parts.answer: push themselves along with their feet (until they can balance)
parts.working: Accept 'learn to balance'.

parts.label: e
parts.text: What is the learners' fee used for?
parts.working: Do not accept 'bicycles' (lent free).

parts.label: f
parts.text: According to Rukhsana, what is the biggest change in her life since learning to ride?
parts.working: Do not accept 'saving money'.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a student who measures a glacier in Hunza, and then answer the questions.

Watching the ice
Twice a year, nineteen-year-old Zainab Karim climbs for six hours to reach the edge of a glacier above her village in Hunza. She carries a measuring tape, a notebook and a small camera, and she photographs the same rocks from exactly the same spot every time.
Zainab began the project at fifteen for a school science competition. Her teacher suggested placing painted stones in a line in front of the glacier and measuring the distance from each stone to the ice. Over four years, the ice has moved back by an average of eleven metres a year.
Glaciers like this one provide water for farming in the valley, especially for the apricot and potato fields. But melting ice also creates dangers. Sometimes water collects in lakes behind loose walls of rock and ice. If these walls break, a flood can rush down the valley with almost no warning.
Zainab now shares her measurements with a university in Islamabad, where scientists compare them with satellite images. 'Satellites can show large changes,' she says, 'but someone still needs to stand here and check the details.'
She is now studying geography and plans to return to Hunza after graduating. She hopes to train other young people in the valley to monitor the glaciers near their own villages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How long does it take Zainab to reach the glacier?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why did Zainab start the project?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Whose idea was it to use painted stones?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which crops in the valley depend on water from the glacier?
parts.working: Both needed.

parts.label: e
parts.text: What can happen if the walls holding back a glacial lake break?
parts.answer: a flood rushes down the valley (with almost no warning)

parts.label: f
parts.text: Why are Zainab's measurements useful to the scientists, even though they have satellite images?
parts.answer: someone needs to check the details on the ground / satellites show only large changes

practice.stem:
Read the article about a school robotics club in Malaysia, and then answer the questions.

The robot that tests the river
When students at a secondary school in Penang, Malaysia, noticed that fish were disappearing from the river behind their school, they decided to find out why. The school's robotics club spent a term building a small floating robot, about the size of a laptop, which they named 'Kingfisher'.
Kingfisher is powered by a solar panel on its top and is steered by remote control from the riverbank. Underneath, it carries sensors that measure the temperature of the water and how much oxygen it contains. Every ten seconds, it sends these readings to a laptop on the bank.
The students quickly discovered that oxygen levels dropped sharply downstream of a pipe from a nearby factory. They presented their results to the local council, which has now asked the factory to treat its waste water before releasing it.
Building the robot was not easy. The first version tipped over in strong currents, so the team added two empty plastic bottles on each side to make it more stable. The total cost of the robot was less than the price of a single scientific sensor bought from a laboratory supplier.
The club's teacher, Mr Lim, says the project has changed how students think about science. 'They used to see it as something in a textbook,' he says. 'Now they see it as a way of solving real problems.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: What made the students want to investigate the river?
parts.answer: fish were disappearing from the river

parts.label: b
parts.text: How is the robot powered?
parts.working: Do not accept 'remote control'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one thing that the sensors measure.
parts.answer: the temperature of the water OR the amount of oxygen in the water
parts.working: Either one.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Where did oxygen levels drop sharply?
parts.answer: downstream of a pipe from a (nearby) factory

parts.label: e
parts.text: What did the team do to make the robot more stable?
parts.answer: added (two) empty plastic bottles on each side

parts.label: f
parts.text: According to Mr Lim, how did students see science before the project?

practice.stem:
Read the article about a truck art workshop in Rawalpindi, and then answer the questions.

Colours on the highway
In a dusty yard near the Grand Trunk Road in Rawalpindi, Muhammad Anwar is painting a peacock on the side of a lorry. Around him, apprentices are fixing hundreds of small metal chains along the front bumper, which will jingle as the vehicle moves.
Anwar learned truck art from his father and has been doing it for thirty-five years. Decorating one lorry completely can take up to three weeks and costs the owner as much as the vehicle earns in two months. 'Drivers spend more time in their trucks than in their homes,' he says. 'They want them to be beautiful.'
Each design tells something about the owner. Pictures of mountains and rivers often remind drivers of their home villages, while lines of poetry painted on the back express their hopes or feelings. Anwar says the most requested image is still the eye, which drivers believe protects them on long journeys.
In recent years, truck art has become fashionable far beyond the highway. Anwar's workshop now receives orders to decorate kettles, furniture and even mobile phone covers, many of them for customers abroad. These small items now earn the workshop more money than the lorries do.
However, Anwar worries about the future. Fewer young people want to spend years learning the skill, and cheaper printed stickers are replacing hand painting on some vehicles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What will the metal chains on the bumper do?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Who taught Anwar truck art?

parts.label: c
parts.text: How long can it take to decorate one lorry?

parts.label: d
parts.text: What do pictures of mountains and rivers often remind drivers of?

parts.label: e
parts.text: What is the most requested image?
parts.working: Do not accept 'peacock'.

parts.label: f
parts.text: What now earns the workshop more money than lorries?
parts.answer: small (decorated) items such as kettles, furniture and phone covers
parts.working: Accept any one example or 'small items'.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a seed bank run by farmers in Nepal, and then answer the questions.

Saving the seeds of the past
In a small stone building in a village in western Nepal, hundreds of glass jars line the shelves. Each one contains seeds: rice, millet, beans, barley and buckwheat, many of them varieties that most farmers stopped growing decades ago.
The community seed bank was set up by a group of twelve farmers led by Kamala Thapa. 'When I was a girl, my mother grew seven kinds of rice,' she says. 'By the time I had my own fields, the shops were selling only two.'
Modern varieties often produce bigger harvests, but they usually need chemical fertiliser and plenty of water. Some of the older varieties are better suited to the region's steep fields. One red rice, for example, grows well in cold water from mountain streams, and a local bean survives long periods without rain.
Farmers can borrow a jar of seeds for free. After the harvest, they must return twice the amount they borrowed, so the bank's collection keeps growing. The seeds are kept dry with ash from cooking fires, a method the farmers' grandparents used.
Last year, when an unusually dry summer destroyed many fields of modern rice, farmers who had planted older varieties from the seed bank still harvested a crop. Since then, demand for the jars has tripled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many farmers set up the seed bank?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many kinds of rice did Kamala's mother grow?
parts.working: Do not accept 'two'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What do modern varieties usually need?
parts.answer: chemical fertiliser and plenty of water
parts.working: Both needed.

parts.label: d
parts.text: What must farmers return after the harvest?
parts.answer: twice the amount (of seed) they borrowed

parts.label: e
parts.text: How are the seeds kept dry?

parts.label: f
parts.text: What happened to the demand for seeds after last year's dry summer?

practice.stem:
Read the article about a potter in Multan who makes blue-glazed pottery, and then answer the questions.

Keeping the blue alive
Ghulam Mustafa's workshop is easy to find: just follow the trail of blue and white dust from the street. For three generations, his family has made the glazed pottery for which Multan is famous.
Unlike most potters, Ghulam does not use a wheel for the large vases. Instead, he builds them by hand from coils of clay, a method that he says gives the walls an even thickness. A vase that stands as tall as a child can take him two weeks to shape.
The designs are painted by his daughter, Saba, who trained as a graphic designer before returning to the family business. She still uses traditional flower patterns, but she has added geometric shapes that appeal to younger buyers.
The most dangerous moment comes during firing. The kiln is heated with wood for about eighteen hours, and if the temperature rises too quickly, a whole week's work can crack. 'You never sleep on firing night,' Ghulam says.
Orders now arrive from as far away as Canada, mostly through Saba's online shop. However, Ghulam worries about the future. Young people in the neighbourhood prefer office jobs, and he has only one apprentice, compared with six when he was a young man.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How can visitors find Ghulam's workshop?
parts.answer: by following the trail of blue and white dust (from the street)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why does Ghulam build large vases from coils of clay?
parts.answer: it gives the walls an even thickness
parts.working: Do not accept 'he has no wheel'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What did Saba do before she joined the family business?
parts.answer: she trained as a graphic designer

parts.label: d
parts.text: What has Saba added to the traditional designs?
parts.working: Do not accept 'flower patterns' (traditional).

parts.label: e
parts.text: What can happen if the kiln heats up too quickly?

parts.label: f
parts.text: How many apprentices did the workshop have when Ghulam was young?
parts.working: Do not accept 'one' (the present number).

practice.stem:
Read the article about a young telescope maker in Ghana, and then answer the questions.

Bringing the stars closer
When Kwame Asante was thirteen, a visiting teacher let his class look at the Moon through a telescope. 'I saw mountains and craters, and I could not sleep that night,' he remembers. Telescopes, however, were far too expensive for his school in a small town in Ghana.
So Kwame decided to build his own. Using old reading-glass lenses and a plastic drainpipe, his first telescope was blurry, but he could make out four tiny dots beside Jupiter. 'Those were its largest moons, and I had found them myself,' he says.
Now nineteen and studying physics at university, Kwame runs workshops in which secondary-school students build simple telescopes from cardboard tubes. Each one costs less than five dollars to make. So far, more than six hundred students have taken part.
The biggest problem is not money but light. Street lamps and lit-up billboards in towns make faint objects almost impossible to see. Kwame therefore organises viewing nights in villages, where the sky is much darker.
His dream is to open a small observatory where students can take photographs of galaxies. He has already been offered a piece of land by a local chief, and he is now trying to raise money for the building.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What did Kwame first see through a telescope?
parts.answer: the Moon (with its mountains and craters)

parts.label: b
parts.text: What did Kwame use to make the tube of his first telescope?
parts.working: Do not accept 'reading-glass lenses' (these were the lenses).

parts.label: c
parts.text: What were the four dots that Kwame saw beside Jupiter?

parts.label: d
parts.text: How much does each telescope made in the workshops cost?
parts.working: Must include 'less than'.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Why are faint objects difficult to see in towns?
parts.working: Do not accept 'money'.

parts.label: f
parts.text: What has a local chief offered Kwame?
parts.answer: a piece of land (for the observatory)

practice.stem:
Read the article about a rescue centre for working donkeys in Karachi, and then answer the questions.

A rest for hard workers
Thousands of donkeys still pull carts through the streets of Karachi, carrying everything from bricks to water tanks. For many families, a single donkey is the only way to earn a living. Yet these animals are often injured, overworked or poorly fed.
A small charity runs a treatment centre near Lyari, where owners can bring their donkeys free of charge. The vet in charge, Dr Mehwish Zaidi, says the most common problem is not illness but badly fitted harnesses. 'A harness that rubs leaves open wounds on the animal's shoulders,' she explains. The centre now makes padded harnesses and sells them at cost price.
Another problem is the heat. In summer, temperatures in the city can pass forty degrees, and donkeys working without shade or water can collapse. The charity has placed water troughs at six busy road junctions.
Owners are also invited to short training sessions on hoof care. At first, few people came, so the charity began giving each owner a free bag of animal feed at the end of the session. Attendance tripled within two months.
Dr Zaidi believes that a healthy donkey is good for everyone. 'When the animal can work, the family can eat,' she says.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How much do owners pay for treatment at the centre?

parts.label: b
parts.text: According to Dr Zaidi, what is the most common problem the centre sees?
parts.working: Do not accept 'illness'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Where on the donkey do open wounds appear?

parts.label: d
parts.text: How has the charity helped donkeys during hot weather?
parts.answer: it has placed water troughs at (six busy road) junctions

parts.label: e
parts.text: What are the training sessions about?

parts.label: f
parts.text: What did the charity do to persuade more owners to attend?
parts.answer: gave each owner a free bag of (animal) feed (at the end)

practice.stem:
Read the article about a woman who runs a guesthouse in Skardu, and then answer the questions.

A room with a view
Shabnam Rizvi never planned to run a guesthouse. Eight years ago, she was working as a schoolteacher in Rawalpindi when her father became ill, and she returned to the family home outside Skardu to look after him.
The house had five empty rooms and a garden full of apricot trees. A friend suggested that she rent the rooms to visitors, and the first guests arrived that summer: a group of cyclists from Japan who had seen a single photograph of the garden online.
Today the guesthouse has nine rooms, and Shabnam employs four people from the village. She insists that everything served at breakfast is local, from the apricot jam to the bread baked in a clay oven. 'Guests can eat cornflakes at home,' she jokes.
Running a business in the mountains is not easy. The road to Skardu is sometimes blocked by landslides, and in winter most tourists stay away. Shabnam uses the quiet months to teach English to village children for free.
Her favourite guests are not the climbers who come to see the famous peaks, but the older travellers who simply sit in the garden for hours. 'They remind me to slow down,' she says.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What was Shabnam's job before she moved to Skardu?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why did she return to the family home?
parts.answer: her father became ill / to look after her father

parts.label: c
parts.text: Where were the first guests from?

parts.label: d
parts.text: How is the bread at the guesthouse baked?

parts.label: e
parts.text: What sometimes blocks the road to Skardu?

parts.label: f
parts.text: What does Shabnam do during the winter months?
parts.answer: teaches English to village children (for free)
parts.working: Do not accept 'closes the guesthouse'.

practice.stem:
Read the article about the lost-property office at a large railway station, and then answer the questions.

Lost and found
Behind a plain door at one of Europe's busiest railway stations is a room that few travellers ever see. Its shelves hold umbrellas by the hundred, piles of coats and scarves, a wheelchair, two violins and, at the moment, a stuffed crocodile almost two metres long.
The lost-property office receives around 400 items every day. Staff record each one on a computer, noting where it was found and adding a short description. Items are kept for three months; after that, most are given to charity, although anything containing personal information, such as laptops, is securely destroyed.
Office manager Elena Rossi has worked there for eleven years. Surprisingly, she says, umbrellas are not the most common item. 'Everyone expects umbrellas,' she laughs, 'but we receive far more phone chargers. People plug them in on the train and simply forget them.' Umbrellas come second, and in winter, gloves move into third place.
Only about a third of all items are ever collected. Elena believes many people do not realise the office exists, while others assume that something left on a train will never be handed in. Items most likely to be reclaimed are wallets and passports; chargers are almost never collected, probably because they are cheap to replace.
The strangest phone call Elena ever received was from a man asking whether anyone had found his false teeth. Someone had.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many items does the office receive each day?

parts.label: b
parts.text: What happens to laptops that are not collected?
parts.working: Do not accept 'given to charity'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which item does the office receive most often?
parts.working: Do not accept 'umbrellas' (second).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which item becomes the third most common in winter?

parts.label: e
parts.text: What proportion of items are collected by their owners?

parts.label: f
parts.text: Why, according to the article, are chargers almost never collected?
parts.working: Do not accept 'people forget them on the train' (explains why they are lost, not why they are not collected).

practice.stem:
Read the article about sleep and teenagers, and then answer the questions.

Why teenagers can't get up
Parents often complain that teenagers stay up too late and then cannot get out of bed in the morning. Many assume this is simply laziness. In fact, scientists say there is a biological explanation.
Everyone has an internal 'body clock' that tells us when to feel sleepy. It is controlled partly by a hormone called melatonin, which the brain releases as it gets dark. In adults and young children, melatonin levels usually rise at around nine or ten in the evening. During the teenage years, however, this happens up to two hours later. A fifteen-year-old who goes to bed at ten may simply lie awake.
Teenagers also need more sleep than adults – between eight and ten hours a night – because their bodies and brains are still developing. When school starts early, many get far less than this. Research shows that tired students find it harder to concentrate and remember information, and they are more likely to feel anxious.
Some schools have experimented with later start times. At one school, moving the start of lessons from 8.00 to 8.50 led to fewer students arriving late and better attendance, although exam results improved only slightly.
Scientists say the most helpful thing teenagers can do themselves is to avoid screens in the hour before bed, because the blue light from phones and tablets delays the release of melatonin even further.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What do many parents believe is the reason teenagers find it hard to get up?

parts.label: b
parts.text: What causes the brain to release melatonin?
parts.working: Accept 'darkness'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: How much later than adults do teenagers' melatonin levels rise?
parts.working: Must include 'up to' or equivalent; accept 'as much as two hours'.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Why do teenagers need more sleep than adults?
parts.answer: their bodies and brains are still developing

parts.label: e
parts.text: What did NOT improve much when one school started lessons later?
parts.working: Do not accept 'attendance' or 'lateness' (these did improve).

parts.label: f
parts.text: Why should teenagers avoid screens before bed?
parts.answer: blue light delays the release of melatonin (even further)

practice.stem:
Read the article about a marine archaeologist, and then answer the questions.

Treasure under the waves
Most people imagine underwater archaeology as a search for gold coins. For Dr Mariam Haddad, the real treasure is usually much less glamorous: broken pots, ship's nails and the bones of animals that sailors ate on long voyages.
Mariam grew up in a fishing town on the coast of Lebanon. As a teenager she wanted to be a doctor, but a summer job helping divers record an old harbour wall changed her mind. She went on to study history and then trained as a professional diver, a process that took longer than her university degree.
Her team is currently studying a trading ship that sank about 1,600 years ago in water forty metres deep. At this depth, divers can work for only about twenty minutes at a time before they must return slowly to the surface. Because of this, every dive is planned carefully, and much of the recording is done with underwater cameras rather than by hand.
The ship's cargo included hundreds of clay jars called amphorae. By studying their shape, the team can tell where they were made, and tiny traces left inside show that most once contained olive oil rather than wine, as the team had first expected.
Mariam says the greatest threat to ancient wrecks today is not the sea but people. Divers who take objects as souvenirs destroy information that can never be recovered.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What did Mariam want to become when she was a teenager?

parts.label: b
parts.text: What experience changed Mariam's mind about her career?
parts.answer: a summer job helping divers record an old harbour wall

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which took Mariam longer: her university degree or her diving training?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Why is every dive at the wreck planned carefully?
parts.answer: divers can work for only about twenty minutes at a time (at that depth)

parts.label: e
parts.text: How can the team tell where the jars were made?
parts.working: Do not accept 'traces left inside' (shows contents).

parts.label: f
parts.text: What did the team discover that surprised them?
parts.answer: most jars contained olive oil (not wine)
parts.working: Must convey olive oil. 'Wine' alone = 0.

practice.stem:
Read the article about mangrove planting on the coast of Sindh, and then answer the questions.

Forests that grow in the sea
Along the coast of the Indus Delta, where the river meets the Arabian Sea, grow forests unlike any others in Pakistan. Mangrove trees stand in salty water on tall, tangled roots, and at high tide only their green tops are visible.
These forests once covered a much larger area. During the twentieth century, dams and canals upstream reduced the amount of fresh water reaching the delta, and many trees were cut down for firewood and to feed camels. Since the 1990s, however, large replanting projects have helped the forests to recover.
Fisherman Ghulam Rasool has planted thousands of young trees himself. He explains that mangroves are important for his work, because many kinds of shrimp and fish spend the first part of their lives sheltering among the roots. 'No mangroves, no fish,' he says simply.
Mangroves also protect the coast. Their roots trap mud and slow down waves, which reduces damage when storms arrive. In addition, scientists have found that mangrove soil stores large amounts of carbon, which helps to limit climate change.
Planting is done in summer, when the soil is soft. Volunteers push seeds or young plants into the mud by hand. Ghulam says the hardest part is not the planting but stopping animals from eating the young shoots during their first year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When are only the tops of the mangrove trees visible?

parts.label: b
parts.text: What reduced the amount of fresh water reaching the delta?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Apart from firewood, why were trees cut down?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Why are mangroves important for Ghulam's work as a fisherman?
parts.answer: shrimp and fish shelter among the roots when young
parts.working: Accept 'young fish/shrimp live among the roots'.

parts.label: e
parts.text: How do mangrove roots reduce storm damage?
parts.answer: they trap mud and slow down waves
parts.working: Accept 'slow down waves' alone.

parts.label: f
parts.text: According to Ghulam, what is the most difficult part of the work?
parts.answer: stopping animals eating the young shoots (in the first year)
parts.working: Do not accept 'planting'.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a professional tea taster in Sri Lanka, and then answer the questions.

A life spent tasting tea
Every morning at nine, Nimal Perera sits down at a long white table on which eighty small cups have been arranged in a line. By lunchtime he will have tasted every one of them. Nimal is a professional tea taster in Colombo, and his judgement helps to decide the price of thousands of kilograms of tea each week.
Tasting is a noisy business. Nimal takes a spoonful of tea and sucks it into his mouth loudly so that it sprays across his tongue, then spits it into a large metal pot. 'Swallowing eighty cups a day would be impossible,' he explains.
Before tasting, he examines the dry leaves and smells the wet leaves left after brewing. Colour matters too: a bright, coppery colour usually means that the tea was processed well. The water is always boiled fresh, because water that has been boiled twice makes tea taste flat.
It took Nimal six years of training before he was allowed to give prices on his own. He avoids spicy food and never wears aftershave, which would interfere with his sense of smell, the most important tool in his job.
Tea from high mountain estates usually sells for the highest prices, as the cool climate makes the leaves grow slowly and develop a stronger flavour. However, Nimal says the weather in the weeks before picking can change the taste more than the height of the estate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many cups of tea does Nimal taste each morning?

parts.label: b
parts.text: What does Nimal do with the tea after tasting it?
parts.answer: spits it into a (large metal) pot

parts.label: c
parts.text: What does a bright, coppery colour usually show?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Why is the water always boiled fresh?
parts.answer: water boiled twice makes tea taste flat

parts.label: e
parts.text: What does Nimal consider the most important tool in his job?
parts.working: Do not accept 'taste' / 'tongue'.

parts.label: f
parts.text: According to Nimal, what can affect the taste of tea more than the height of the estate?
parts.answer: the weather in the weeks before picking

practice.stem:
Read the article about a camel-milk dairy in the Thar Desert, and then answer the questions.

Ice cream from the desert
For centuries, herders in the Thar Desert have relied on camels for transport and milk. Until recently, however, the milk was used only by their own families, because it spoils quickly in the heat and there was no way to get it to city markets before it went sour.
That changed when Dr Kavita Kumari, a vet who grew up near Mithi, persuaded a charity to buy a small milk-cooling tank powered by solar panels. Herders now bring their milk to a collection point every morning, where it is tested for quality and chilled to 4 °C within two hours of milking.
Camel milk is saltier than cow's milk and contains less fat. It also has more vitamin C, which is valuable in a region where fresh fruit is scarce. Some people who cannot digest cow's milk find camel milk easier to drink, although Dr Kumari is careful not to claim that it cures any illness.
The dairy's best-selling product, surprisingly, is not milk but ice cream. It is flavoured with cardamom and sold in Karachi cafés, where customers pay almost four times the price of the raw milk used to make it.
The extra income has changed life for many herding families. Several now keep their children in school instead of sending them to look after the animals. The biggest remaining problem is the road: during the monsoon, the track to the main highway sometimes floods, and deliveries are delayed for days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Why was camel milk not sold in city markets in the past?
parts.answer: it spoils quickly in the heat / went sour before reaching markets

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is Dr Kumari's profession?

parts.label: c
parts.text: How is the milk-cooling tank powered?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which vitamin is found in greater amounts in camel milk?

parts.label: e
parts.text: What is the dairy's best-selling product?
parts.working: Do not accept 'milk'.

parts.label: f
parts.text: What is the biggest remaining problem for the dairy?
parts.answer: the road / the track floods in the monsoon (and deliveries are delayed)

practice.stem:
Read the article about a solar lamp scheme in an old city lane, and then answer the questions.

A lamp for the lane
At the end of a narrow lane in an old quarter of Multan, there is still no streetlight. The electricity cable was never extended this far, so residents used to walk home in the dark, and many were afraid to go out after sunset.
Last year, a retired electrician, Mr Rafiq Lodhi, built a lamp that charges during the day from a solar panel fixed to the wall. The lamp switches on automatically at sunset. The residents paid for the parts through a small monthly contribution from each household.
The first lamp worked well for two months. In the monsoon, however, the panel was often covered by dust and cloud, and the lamp switched off before midnight. Mr Lodhi now cleans the panel every week, and he has fitted a battery to store extra power for cloudy days.
Residents say that the lane feels safer. 'We used to be afraid to walk to the mosque,' says one woman. 'Now we walk together.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Why has the lane never had a streetlight?
parts.answer: the electricity cable was never extended to the lane
parts.working: Accept 'there is no electricity cable' in the lane. Do not accept 'the lamps are too expensive' (not stated).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Who built the lamp?
parts.answer: a retired electrician, Mr Rafiq Lodhi
parts.working: Accept 'Mr Lodhi'. Do not accept 'the residents' (they paid for it).

parts.label: c
parts.text: When does the lamp switch on?
parts.working: Accept 'at sunset'. Do not accept 'before midnight' (when it switched off in the monsoon).

parts.label: d
parts.text: How did the residents pay for the parts?
parts.answer: a small monthly contribution from each household
parts.working: Accept 'a monthly contribution' or 'each household paid a little every month'.

parts.label: e
parts.text: What caused the lamp to switch off before midnight in the monsoon?
parts.answer: the solar panel was covered by dust and cloud
parts.working: Accept either 'dust on the panel' or 'cloud covering the panel'. Do not accept 'the battery was empty' (the battery was added later).

parts.label: f
parts.text: What did Mr Lodhi add to the lamp?
parts.answer: a battery (to store extra power for cloudy days)
parts.working: Accept 'a battery'. Do not accept 'a second solar panel' (not stated).

practice.stem:
Read the article about an apprentice clockmaker in Switzerland, and then answer the questions.

Time on her hands
At twenty, Lea Brunner is the youngest of the eleven craftspeople at a small watch-repair workshop in a Swiss mountain town. She is halfway through a four-year apprenticeship, during which she spends three days a week at the workbench and two at a technical college.
Her interest started not with watches but with a broken music box that belonged to her grandmother. 'I took it apart when I was ten and couldn't put it back together,' she admits. 'My grandmother wasn't angry; she found an old clockmaker who showed me how it worked.'
The work demands extraordinary patience. Some parts are thinner than a human hair and are handled with tweezers under a magnifying lens. Lea's teacher made her file a single brass wheel for a whole week before she was allowed to work on a real customer's watch. 'He wanted me to stop thinking that speed matters,' she explains.
Many people assume that mechanical watches have no future now that phones show the time. Lea disagrees. The workshop has more orders than ever, she says, because people want objects that can be repaired for generations rather than thrown away after a few years.
After her apprenticeship, Lea hopes to spend a year working in Japan, where she believes some of the most skilled watch restorers in the world are based, before returning to open her own workshop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many days a week does Lea spend at college?
parts.working: Do not accept three (workbench days).

parts.label: b
parts.text: What object first made Lea interested in mechanisms?
parts.working: Do not accept 'a watch'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What does Lea use to see the smallest parts?
parts.working: Do not accept 'tweezers' (used to hold them).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Why did her teacher make her file one wheel for a week?
parts.answer: to stop her thinking that speed matters / to teach her patience

parts.label: e
parts.text: According to Lea, why does the workshop have more orders than ever?
parts.answer: people want objects that can be repaired for generations (instead of being thrown away)

parts.label: f
parts.text: What does Lea plan to do immediately after her apprenticeship?
parts.working: Do not accept 'open her own workshop' (that comes later).

practice.stem:
Read the article about a project that counts butterflies in the Margalla Hills, and then answer the questions.

Counting wings
Once a fortnight, between March and October, a group of volunteers walks the same two-kilometre path through the Margalla Hills near Islamabad. They move slowly, notebook in hand, recording every butterfly that crosses an imaginary box five metres wide in front of them.
The project was started by Dr Faiza Hayat, an ecologist, who explains why butterflies matter. 'They react quickly to changes in temperature and plant life,' she says, 'so a fall in their numbers is often an early warning that something is wrong with the whole habitat.'
Volunteers need no scientific background, but they must attend a half-day course in identification. The hardest skill, according to most of them, is not recognising the species but resisting the temptation to count the same butterfly twice when it circles back.
Counts are only carried out when the temperature is above seventeen degrees and the wind is light, because butterflies rarely fly in cold or windy conditions. If a volunteer misses a week, the rule is that the walk is not repeated later, so that the dates remain comparable from year to year.
After five seasons, the data show an interesting pattern: some species are appearing about ten days earlier in spring than when the project began. Dr Hayat is careful not to draw conclusions too soon. 'Five years is a short time in nature,' she warns.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How often do the volunteers walk the path?
parts.answer: once a fortnight / every two weeks (from March to October)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why does Dr Hayat think a fall in butterfly numbers matters?
parts.answer: it is (often) an early warning that something is wrong with the (whole) habitat

parts.label: c
parts.text: What must volunteers do before they can take part?

parts.label: d
parts.text: What do most volunteers find the hardest skill?
parts.answer: not counting the same butterfly twice (when it circles back)
parts.working: Do not accept 'recognising species'.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Why are walks missed by a volunteer not repeated later?
parts.answer: so that the dates remain comparable from year to year

parts.label: f
parts.text: What change in some species have the volunteers noticed?
parts.answer: they appear (about ten days) earlier in spring
parts.working: Do not accept 'numbers have fallen'.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a team that restores old films for an archive in Lahore, and then answer the questions.

Saving the silver screen
In a cool, windowless basement in Lahore, a team of six technicians is racing against time. On metal shelves around them sit more than two thousand cans of film, some of them holding movies that were made in the 1950s and have not been seen for decades.
The greatest enemy is not age but vinegar. Older film was made of a material that slowly breaks down in warm, damp air, giving off a sharp, sour smell. Once this process starts, the film shrinks and curls, and eventually it can no longer be played. For this reason the basement is kept at fourteen degrees, and every can is checked with a small paper strip that changes colour when the decay begins.
Each film is first cleaned by hand with soft cloths, a job that can take three days for a long feature. The frames are then scanned one by one by a machine that the team calls 'the patient giant' because it handles each frame so slowly.
The team's leader, Umer Qadri, says the most rewarding moments come when relatives of the original actors visit. 'Last month a woman of eighty saw her mother dancing on screen for the first time,' he says. 'She had only ever seen still photographs.'
The archive receives no regular government money. It survives on donations and on fees from television channels that pay to show the restored films.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many cans of film are kept in the basement?
parts.working: Must include 'more than'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is the first sign that a film is decaying?
parts.working: Accept 'it smells of vinegar'. Do not accept 'it shrinks' (later effect).

parts.label: c
parts.text: At what temperature is the basement kept?

parts.label: d
parts.text: What is used to show that decay has started in a can?
parts.answer: a (small) paper strip that changes colour

parts.label: e
parts.text: Why do the team call the scanner 'the patient giant'?

parts.label: f
parts.text: Apart from donations, how does the archive get money?
parts.answer: fees from television channels (that show the restored films)
parts.working: Do not accept 'the government'.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a girls' cricket academy in Multan, and then answer the questions.

Bowling towards a dream
When the Multan Girls' Cricket Academy opened four years ago, only eleven girls came to the first practice – just enough for one team. Today it trains more than ninety players aged between ten and eighteen.
The academy was founded by Farah Qureshi, a former fast bowler who played for her province. 'When I was young, I practised with my brothers in the street, but I had no coach and no proper equipment,' she says. 'I wanted girls today to have a better start.'
Training takes place four afternoons a week on a ground lent by a local college. Players work on fitness, batting and bowling, and they also attend talks on healthy eating. The academy provides bats, pads and helmets, which are paid for by a sports shop in the city and by small donations from parents.
Persuading families was the hardest part at first. Some parents worried about their daughters' safety travelling to practice, so the academy arranged a minibus that collects players from three points in the city. Others were concerned about exams, so the girls now have a supervised homework session for an hour before training starts.
Two former players have already been selected for national youth squads. Farah says she is just as proud of the girls who have become more confident at school and in their communities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many girls came to the first practice?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO things the players do at the academy apart from batting and bowling.
parts.answer: 1. work on fitness 2. attend talks on healthy eating
parts.working: 1 mark each. (Supervised homework also acceptable as a third option.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Who pays for the equipment? Give TWO answers.
parts.answer: 1. a sports shop in the city 2. (small donations from) parents
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept 'the college' (lends the ground).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO worries that parents had, and say how the academy dealt with each one.
parts.answer: Safety travelling to practice → minibus collecting players from three points; exams / schoolwork → supervised homework session for an hour before training
parts.working: 1 mark for each worry, 1 mark for each matching solution.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a rooftop school garden in Singapore, and then answer the questions.

A farm on the fourth floor
Space is precious in Singapore, so when a primary school in the east of the city wanted a garden, it had only one place to go: up. The flat roof of the school's four-storey building is now home to more than fifty large planting boxes.
Pupils grow pak choi, spinach, tomatoes, chillies, lemongrass and several herbs. Each class is responsible for its own box and must water it, remove weeds and record how fast the plants are growing in a notebook. Older pupils also test the soil and decide when it needs compost.
Most of the vegetables are used in the school canteen, where cooks prepare them for lunch at least twice a week. Anything left over is sold to parents at a small stall on Friday afternoons, and the money is used to buy new seeds.
Teachers say the garden has helped pupils in several ways. Children who once refused to eat green vegetables now try the ones they have grown. Mathematics lessons use real measurements from the plants, and pupils who struggle in the classroom often shine in the garden.
There have been challenges. On hot afternoons, the roof can become extremely warm, so some plants are protected by shade nets. Strong winds during storms once blew several boxes over, and they are now fixed to the floor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many floors does the school building have?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give THREE things each class must do for its planting box.
parts.answer: 1. water it 2. remove weeds 3. record how fast the plants grow (in a notebook)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not credit testing the soil or deciding about compost (done by older pupils only).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give TWO ways the garden has helped pupils, according to teachers.
parts.answer: Any two: children try green vegetables they have grown; maths lessons use real measurements; pupils who struggle in class shine in the garden
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO problems the garden has had.
parts.answer: 1. the roof becomes extremely warm / too hot (on hot afternoons) 2. strong winds blew boxes over
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept solutions only if linked to the problem.

practice.stem:
Read the article about electric rickshaws in Bangladesh and Pakistan, and then answer the questions.

The quiet tuk-tuk
For many years, the noisy, smoky auto-rickshaw has been a familiar sight in South Asian cities. Now a quieter version is spreading. Electric rickshaws, powered by batteries instead of petrol or diesel engines, are becoming common in cities such as Dhaka and are being tested in Karachi and Lahore.
Drivers say the biggest advantage is cost. Charging a battery overnight costs much less than filling a tank with fuel, and electric motors have fewer moving parts, so repairs are cheaper too. Passengers like the fact that the ride is smoother and that they can hold a conversation without shouting.
Electric rickshaws also help the environment. Because they produce no exhaust fumes on the street, they improve air quality in crowded areas, and they reduce noise pollution.
However, there are problems. The batteries are heavy and expensive to replace, and most last only two or three years. Many drivers charge them at home using unsafe wiring, which can cause fires. In some cities, the extra demand for electricity at night has put pressure on the power supply.
Some companies are now building solar charging stations where drivers can exchange an empty battery for a full one in less than five minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What are the new rickshaws powered by?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO reasons why electric rickshaws are cheaper for drivers.
parts.answer: 1. charging costs less than fuel 2. fewer moving parts so repairs are cheaper
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give TWO things passengers like about electric rickshaws.
parts.answer: 1. the ride is smoother 2. they can talk without shouting / it is quieter
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE problems with electric rickshaws.
parts.answer: Any three: batteries heavy; batteries expensive to replace; batteries last only two or three years; charging at home with unsafe wiring can cause fires; extra demand for electricity puts pressure on power supply
parts.working: 1 mark each. 'Heavy and expensive' counts as two points only if both stated clearly.

practice.stem:
Read the article about an app that reduces food waste, and then answer the questions.

An app against waste
