Every evening, bakeries, cafés and supermarkets throw away food that is still perfectly good to eat, simply because it will not be fresh enough to sell the next day. A group of university students in Islamabad decided to do something about it.
Their mobile phone app, called 'Bachat', lists shops that have surplus food at the end of the day. Customers can reserve a 'surprise bag' for about a third of the normal price and collect it during a time slot, usually in the last hour before the shop closes. They do not know exactly what will be inside, which many users say is part of the fun.
Shop owners like the app because they earn some money from food that would otherwise be wasted, and they attract new customers who may come back to buy at full price. Some also donate bags to a local orphanage through the app.
Since its launch eighteen months ago, the app has been downloaded more than 60,000 times, and over 200 businesses have joined. The founders estimate that it has saved around 90 tonnes of food from being thrown away.
The team now hopes to expand to Lahore and Peshawar, and to add home-cooked meals from small family kitchens.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When do customers usually collect their bags?
parts.answer: in the last hour before the shop closes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO details about the 'surprise bags'.
parts.answer: Any two: cost about a third of the normal price; reserved through the app; customers do not know what is inside
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give TWO reasons why shop owners like the app.
parts.answer: 1. they earn money from food that would be wasted 2. they attract new customers (who may return)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO plans the team has for the future.
parts.answer: 1. expand to Lahore and Peshawar 2. add home-cooked meals from family kitchens
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a tool library in Multan, and then answer the questions.

Borrow, don't buy
In a small room in an old lane in Multan, a wall of shelves holds hammers, drills, saws and a ladder. Anyone who needs a tool can borrow it for a week at a time.
The library was set up by Ahsan Raza, a carpenter who noticed that many families bought tools that they used only once or twice a year. 'Why spend a fortune on a drill that sits in a cupboard?' he asks.
Members pay a yearly fee and sign a card each time they borrow something. If a tool is returned damaged, the member must repair it or pay for the repair, but Ahsan says this has happened only twice.
On Thursday evenings, volunteers teach basic repair skills. Many of the students are young women who want to fix furniture in their own homes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO kinds of tool that the library lends.
parts.answer: hammers; drills; saws; a ladder (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept 'shelves' or 'the room'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO things a member must do to borrow a tool.
parts.answer: pay a yearly fee; sign a card each time they borrow (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept 'learn repair skills' (the Thursday classes are not needed to borrow).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Who set up the tool library?
parts.working: Accept 'Ahsan Raza'. Do not accept 'the volunteers'.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE details about the Thursday classes or about damaged tools.
parts.answer: volunteers teach basic repair skills on Thursday evenings; many of the students are young women; they want to fix furniture in their own homes; a damaged tool must be repaired or paid for (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three correct details from the text.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a women's co-operative in Hunza, and then answer the questions.

Drying the harvest
In the autumn, the apricot orchards around Karimabad are heavy with fruit, and the women of the Gulmit Women's Co-operative have only a few weeks to make the most of it. Their work begins when the fruit is picked, sorted and washed.
Some apricots are eaten fresh in the villages. Others are laid out on mats on the flat roofs of the houses, where the dry mountain air and strong sun turn them into soft, sweet dried fruit within about ten days. Cracked apricot kernels are also collected and sold.
The co-operative was set up after a bad harvest, when families were struggling to earn money. It now sells dried apricots, apricot oil and jam in Gilgit and at tourist shops in Karimabad. The women decide together how the profits are shared, and part of the money pays for a school bus.
To keep the fruit clean, the women cover the mats with fine nets to keep out birds and insects, and they turn the apricots by hand every day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO products that the co-operative sells.
parts.answer: dried apricots; apricot oil; apricot jam (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Fresh apricots are eaten in the villages, not sold.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO ways in which the women keep the drying fruit clean.
parts.answer: cover the mats with fine nets (to keep out birds and insects); turn the apricots by hand every day
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'nets' alone only if linked to birds or insects.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give TWO details about how the apricots are dried.
parts.answer: laid out on mats; on flat roofs; in dry mountain air and strong sun; takes about ten days (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE facts about the co-operative from the article.
parts.answer: set up after a bad harvest; sells in Gilgit and in tourist shops in Karimabad; women decide together how profits are shared; money pays for a school bus (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three correct facts.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a solar water kiosk in a village in Tharparkar, and then answer the questions.

Clean water, close to home
For years, the women of Chachro village walked for almost an hour each morning to fetch water from a well that was often dry. Now a small solar-powered kiosk stands in the centre of the village, and water is available all day.
The kiosk has a tank on its roof, which fills from a borehole. Solar panels power a pump that works even on cloudy days, and the water passes through a filter before it reaches the taps. Each family pays a small amount for every container they collect.
The project was planned by a local engineer, Imran Bhatti, with help from the district council. Villagers were asked to choose the position of the kiosk, and they picked a spot near the school so that children could also fetch water on their way home.
The kiosk needs to be cleaned every month. A group of three young men from the village has been trained to do this and to repair the pump when it breaks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO reasons why the women no longer need to walk to the old well.
parts.answer: there is a kiosk in the village centre; water is available all day (any two details / reasons)
parts.working: Accept 'the old well was often dry' as an alternative. Give 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO parts of the kiosk system that are mentioned in the article.
parts.answer: a tank on the roof; solar panels; a pump; a filter (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Who planned the project?
parts.answer: a local engineer, Imran Bhatti (with help from the district council)
parts.working: Do not accept 'the villagers' (they chose the position).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE details about how the kiosk is maintained or paid for.
parts.answer: cleaned every month; cleaned and repaired by a group of three trained young men; the pump is repaired when it breaks; each family pays a small amount for each container (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three correct details.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a community swimming pool in Lahore, and then answer the questions.

A pool for everyone
The old public pool in a Lahore neighbourhood had been closed for six years. Last spring, a group of residents raised enough money to repair the tiles and to replace the pump, and the pool reopened in time for the summer holidays.
The pool is now open to families in the morning and to women only in the afternoon. Children under ten must be in the water with an adult, and everyone must shower before entering. The lifeguard checks the water every hour and records the results in a book by the gate.
The reopening was welcomed by parents, who said there was nowhere safe for their children to swim. Lessons are given on Tuesdays and Thursdays by a trained instructor, and the first course was fully booked within a week.
The residents plan to ask the city council for money to build a small changing room, which many visitors have asked for.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO things the residents did to reopen the pool.
parts.answer: raised money; repaired the tiles; replaced the pump (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO rules that visitors must follow.
parts.answer: children under ten must be in the water with an adult; everyone must shower before entering (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. The afternoon women-only arrangement is a timing rule, so accept it too.

parts.label: c
parts.text: How often does the lifeguard check the water?
parts.working: Accept 'hourly'.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE details about the swimming lessons or the residents' plans.
parts.answer: lessons on Tuesdays and Thursdays; given by a trained instructor; the first course was fully booked within a week; the residents plan to ask for a small changing room (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three correct details.

practice.stem:
Read the article about repair cafés, and then answer the questions.

Don't throw it away – fix it!
On the first Saturday of every month, a community hall in Utrecht in the Netherlands fills with broken things: toasters that will not toast, jeans with torn pockets, bicycles with flat tyres and lamps that refuse to light. Their owners have come to a repair café, where volunteers help them fix their belongings for free.
The idea began in Amsterdam in 2009 and has since spread to thousands of towns around the world, including several in Pakistan and India. Volunteers are usually retired engineers, tailors, carpenters and electricians who enjoy sharing their skills.
Visitors do not simply hand over their item and wait. Instead, they sit beside the volunteer and help with the repair, so that they can do it themselves next time. While they wait for a free table, they can have tea and biscuits and chat with neighbours.
Organisers say about two-thirds of items are successfully repaired. The most common reason for failure is that spare parts are no longer available, or that the item has been glued together in the factory so that it cannot be opened without breaking it.
Supporters of repair cafés say they reduce the amount of rubbish sent to landfill, save people money and bring communities together. Some campaigners also hope they will put pressure on manufacturers to design products that last longer and are easier to repair.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO kinds of volunteers who usually work at repair cafés.
parts.answer: Any two: retired engineers; tailors; carpenters; electricians
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO things visitors do while waiting for a table.
parts.answer: 1. have tea and biscuits 2. chat with neighbours
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Why do visitors help with the repair?
parts.answer: so that they can do it themselves next time

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO reasons why some items cannot be repaired.
parts.answer: 1. spare parts are no longer available 2. the item has been glued together in the factory / cannot be opened without breaking
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Give THREE benefits of repair cafés, according to supporters.
parts.answer: 1. reduce rubbish sent to landfill 2. save people money 3. bring communities together
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not credit 'pressure on manufacturers' (a hope of some campaigners, not a benefit stated by supporters).

practice.stem:
Read the article about a high-altitude porter in Gilgit-Baltistan, and then answer the questions.

Carrying the mountain
Each summer, thousands of climbers and trekkers travel to the mountains of Gilgit-Baltistan, hoping to see K2 and the other giants of the Karakoram. Few of them would get far without people like Ali Hussain.
Ali, aged thirty-four, has worked as a porter for sixteen years. On a typical trek to K2 base camp, he carries up to twenty-five kilograms of food, tents and fuel on his back for about eight days each way. The route crosses rivers, steep rocky paths and the Baltoro Glacier, where deep cracks in the ice can be hidden under snow.
Porters face many dangers. The altitude can cause headaches, sickness and breathlessness, and sudden storms can bring freezing winds. In the past, porters were often given poor equipment, and some suffered frostbite. Today, rules require trekking companies to provide boots, warm jackets and sunglasses, and to pay insurance.
The work is well paid compared with farming, and Ali has used his earnings to send his three children to school in Skardu. However, the season lasts only from June to September, so in winter he repairs houses and looks after his family's animals.
Ali's ambition is to become a licensed mountain guide. He has started learning English from trekkers in the evenings and has taken a first-aid course run by a climbing club.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How much does Ali carry on a typical trek?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO things Ali carries.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give TWO effects that altitude can have on porters.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO things that trekking companies must now provide.
parts.answer: Any two: boots; warm jackets; sunglasses; insurance
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Give TWO things Ali is doing to help him become a guide.
parts.answer: 1. learning English (from trekkers) 2. taking a first-aid course
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Read the article about coral reef restoration in the Maldives, and then answer the questions.

Gardeners of the reef
Beneath the turquoise water around the Maldives lie some of the world's most beautiful coral reefs. But in recent years, rising sea temperatures have caused large areas of coral to turn white and die, a process known as 'bleaching'.
Marine biologist Aminath Shareef leads a project that is trying to help reefs recover. Her team collects small pieces of healthy coral that have broken off naturally during storms. They tie these to metal frames shaped like tables, which are placed on the sea floor about eight metres below the surface. Over the next two years, the pieces grow and eventually join together to form new reef.
The project depends on local people. Fishermen report where storms have broken coral, and hotel guests can pay to 'adopt' a frame, which pays for materials. Students from island schools help to clean the frames, removing seaweed that would otherwise block the sunlight the coral needs.
Aminath is careful to explain that restoration alone cannot save the reefs. 'We can repair small areas,' she says, 'but unless the world reduces the gases that are warming the oceans, bleaching will keep happening.'
Even so, the frames have already brought results. Divers have counted more fish around the restored sites, and some of the new coral has survived a recent heatwave that bleached nearby natural reef.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What has caused coral to turn white and die?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO details about the frames the team uses.
parts.answer: Any two: made of metal; shaped like tables; placed on the sea floor; about eight metres below the surface
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give THREE ways in which local people help the project.
parts.answer: 1. fishermen report where coral has broken 2. hotel guests pay to adopt a frame 3. students clean the frames / remove seaweed
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO results that show the project is working.
parts.answer: 1. divers have counted more fish around the restored sites 2. some new coral survived a heatwave (that bleached nearby reef)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Read the article about life at a research station in Antarctica, and then answer the questions.

Winter at the bottom of the world
When the last supply plane leaves the research station in late February, the twenty-two people who stay behind know they will not see anyone else for eight months. Antarctic winter is arriving, and for weeks the sun will not rise at all.
Station doctor Priya Nair is spending her first winter on the ice. As well as treating injuries, she must be ready to act as a dentist and even to perform simple operations, as no aircraft can land in the darkness and extreme cold.
The scientists at the station study the atmosphere, the ice sheet and the stars. Some collect air samples to measure pollution; others drill deep into the ice, where tiny bubbles of ancient air reveal what the climate was like thousands of years ago.
Keeping spirits up is just as important as the science. The team eats dinner together every evening, takes turns cooking and celebrates every birthday. On Saturday nights there is a film or a quiz. Priya says the hardest thing is the lack of fresh fruit and vegetables, although a small greenhouse produces lettuce and herbs under special lights.
Despite the challenges, she has no regrets. 'When the southern lights fill the sky in green and purple,' she says, 'you forget the cold completely.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: How long will the team not see anyone else?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO jobs Priya must be ready to do, apart from treating injuries.
parts.answer: 1. act as a dentist 2. perform simple operations
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give THREE things the scientists study.
parts.answer: 1. the atmosphere 2. the ice sheet 3. the stars
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'pollution' for atmosphere, 'ancient climate' for ice.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO ways in which the team keeps spirits up.
parts.answer: Any two: eating dinner together; taking turns cooking; celebrating birthdays; film or quiz on Saturday nights
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a community language café in Peshawar, and then answer the questions.

Talking across the table
On Sunday afternoons, the upstairs room of a bookshop on Saddar Road fills with people speaking to each other in four or five languages. The café is called Lafz, which means 'word', and it was started by a group of teachers who wanted people to practise speaking without the pressure of a classroom.
The rules are simple. Each table has a sign showing the language that should be spoken there. Newcomers are asked to sit with someone who is slightly more confident, and there is always a volunteer who can help when a conversation stops.
Some visitors come to learn Pashto, Arabic or English. Others are refugees and new residents who want to make friends. The organisers say that the most surprising result is how many regular visitors now teach each other their own languages.
The café charges a small entry fee, which pays for tea and biscuits and for printed word lists. Anyone who cannot pay can join for free by helping to set up the tables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO features of the café that help people to speak without pressure.
parts.answer: no classroom atmosphere / no pressure; each table has a language sign; newcomers sit with a more confident speaker; a volunteer helps when conversation stops (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept 'the café is on Sunday' (not a feature of pressure).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO reasons why people come to the café.
parts.answer: to learn a language (Pashto, Arabic or English); to make friends (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'refugees and new residents' only if the reason is given.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What is the entry fee used to buy?
parts.answer: tea and biscuits and printed word lists
parts.working: Accept any one of these; the answer 'the rent' is not in the text.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE details about the café's rules or its visitors.
parts.answer: each table has a language sign; newcomers sit with a more confident speaker; a volunteer is always there to help; regular visitors teach each other their languages (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three correct details from the text.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a school recycling project in Hyderabad, and then answer the questions.

From bottles to benches
When Class 10 at a boys' high school in Hyderabad was asked to design a project, the students chose a problem they could see every day: plastic bottles left in the school yard. They set out to show that the bottles could be useful.
The students collected bottles from every classroom and cleaned them carefully. Then they cut the bottles into strips, melted the strips in a simple oven and pressed the soft plastic into flat boards. The boards were used to make a bench and a set of planters for the garden.
The project was not easy. Some of the first boards cracked, and the team had to test different temperatures. Their teacher, Mr Javed Lashari, said that the biggest lesson was patience. 'They wanted it to work straight away,' he says, 'but real science takes time.'
Now the rest of the school has joined in. Each class collects its own bottles, and the team has promised to make a new bench for the playground at the end of the term.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO steps the students took to prepare the bottles.
parts.answer: collected bottles from every classroom; cleaned them carefully; cut them into strips (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Melting and pressing come later in the process.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO things the students made from the plastic boards.
parts.answer: a bench; a set of planters for the garden (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What problem did the students find in the early stages?
parts.answer: some of the first boards cracked
parts.working: Accept 'they had to test different temperatures' only as the response to the problem.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE things that the article says about the rest of the school or the future of the project.
parts.answer: each class now collects its own bottles; the rest of the school has joined in; the team has promised a new playground bench at the end of term; the lesson is patience (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Mr Lashari's comment about patience is a lesson, not a plan for the future, so accept it only as one of three valid points.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a night-time museum tour in Karachi, and then answer the questions.

A museum after dark
The Maritime Heritage Museum in Karachi is best known for its old fishing boats and its displays about the port. Once a month, however, it stays open late, and visitors can explore the galleries by torchlight.
The tours are led by former students of the museum's education programme. Each guide prepares a short story about one object, such as a hand-carved oar or an old ship's lantern. The guides say that the stories are often more memorable when the lights are low.
Tickets must be bought in advance online, because the number of visitors is limited to forty for safety reasons. Children under twelve must be accompanied by an adult, and the museum asks that mobile phones are switched off during the tour.
The money from the night tours pays for a repair fund that keeps the boats in good condition. Last year it paid for a new roof on the old warehouse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO things that the museum is known for.
parts.answer: its old fishing boats; its displays about the port (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. The night tours are not what the museum is best known for.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO rules for the night tour.
parts.answer: tickets must be bought in advance online; children under twelve need an adult; mobile phones must be switched off (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. The limit of forty visitors is a rule for safety, so it is also acceptable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What do the guides prepare for each visit?
parts.answer: a short story about one object
parts.working: Accept 'a short story about an object'.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE details about the night tours or the money they raise.
parts.answer: led by former students of the education programme; each guide prepares a story about one object; tickets must be bought in advance online; visitors are limited to forty; the money pays for a repair fund (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three correct details from the text.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a blood donation drive in Rawalpindi, and then answer the questions.

Give, and keep giving
Every month, a small group of volunteers sets up a blood donation tent outside a large hospital in Rawalpindi. Many donors arrive during their lunch break, while others come straight from work or after evening prayers.
Before donating, each person is asked about their health and is given a quick check of their blood pressure and iron level. Donors are advised to drink plenty of water and to eat a light meal the same day. After the donation, they rest for ten minutes and are offered juice and biscuits.
The drive was started by a nurse, Shazia Mehmood, after she saw how often patients needed blood during an emergency. She believes that most healthy adults could give blood at least twice a year without any risk.
The volunteers say that the hardest part is persuading people to come back. They now send a text message to every donor three months later, with a short thank-you and a reminder of the date of the next drive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO things each donor is asked or checked before donating.
parts.answer: questions about their health; a check of blood pressure; a check of iron level (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO pieces of advice given to donors on the day of their donation.
parts.answer: drink plenty of water; eat a light meal (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Why did Shazia Mehmood start the drive?
parts.answer: she saw how often patients needed blood during an emergency
parts.working: Accept 'to help patients in emergencies'.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE details about how the volunteers keep donors coming back.
parts.answer: they send a text message to every donor three months later; the message is a thank-you; it includes a reminder of the next drive date (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'they find it hardest to persuade people to return' as background, not as a detail of the method.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a rural bus service in Balochistan, and then answer the questions.

The bus that waits
For the people of a remote valley in northern Balochistan, the bus to the district town leaves only twice a week. Until recently, the journey was so unreliable that many families gave up waiting and walked instead.
The new service runs on a timetable that is printed on the side of each bus, and passengers can book a seat by sending a short message to a phone number at the bus stop. The drivers have also agreed to wait five minutes at the last village if a passenger is running late.
The project was funded by the district government and by a charity that supports rural schools. The charity asked for the buses to stop at the girls' school, so that students can attend classes in the town on Saturdays.
Local people are happy with the change, but they still want more buses. A council member says that the next step is to offer a night service for patients travelling to hospital.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO features of the new bus service that make it more reliable.
parts.answer: a printed timetable on the side of each bus; passengers can book a seat by message; drivers wait five minutes for late passengers (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Who paid for the new service?
parts.answer: the district government and a charity that supports rural schools
parts.working: 2 marks for both; 1 mark for one only.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Why did the charity ask for the bus to stop at the girls' school?
parts.answer: so that students can attend classes in the town on Saturdays
parts.working: 1 mark. Do not accept 'the school is near the bus stop' (not stated).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE details about how the bus service is booked or timed, or what local people want next.
parts.answer: timetable printed on the side of each bus; book a seat by sending a short message; drivers wait five minutes for late passengers; local people want more buses; a night service for patients (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three correct details from the text.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a robotics club in Karachi, and then answer the questions.

Building in the lunch break
The robotics club at a girls' college in Karachi began with one old computer and a box of motors that a teacher had found in a store cupboard. Today, the club has three workshops and a team that enters national competitions each year.
Members meet in the lunch break and after school. Older students mentor the younger ones, and every new member must complete a small project before joining the competition team. The projects range from a light-sensing toy car to a simple machine that sorts coloured beads.
The club's biggest success came last year, when its team built a robot that could carry water across a sandy course. The judges were impressed by how the girls had designed the wheels to grip the sand.
The club is looking for sponsors, because the parts for the robots are expensive. Its members hope to buy a three-dimensional printer, which would make it easier to build new parts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO things the club had when it first began.
parts.answer: one old computer; a box of motors (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. The three workshops came later.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO ways in which the club is organised.
parts.answer: older students mentor younger ones; members meet at lunch and after school (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What must new members do before they can join the competition team?
parts.working: Accept 'a small project'.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE details about the club's success or its future plans.
parts.answer: robot carried water across a sandy course; judges praised the wheel design; looking for sponsors; hope to buy a three-dimensional printer (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of the four points.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a day trip to a salt mine, and then answer the questions.

Underground in Khewra
The Khewra salt mine, which lies about two hours from Islamabad, is one of the largest salt mines in the world. Visitors enter through a narrow tunnel and walk down a long set of stairs into a network of rooms carved from rock salt.
Guides explain how the salt was formed millions of years ago, when an ancient sea dried up. They also show visitors a small mosque, a hall with a salt-crystal ceiling and a row of statues carved entirely from salt.
The mine is cool all year round, which makes it a popular place to visit in the summer. Visitors are advised to wear comfortable shoes, because the floors are uneven, and to bring a light jacket for the cooler corridors.
Because the mine is so popular, the owners have recently added a small café near the entrance. Some visitors, however, say that the walk back up the stairs is the most tiring part of the trip.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO features of the mine that are shown to visitors.
parts.answer: a small mosque; a hall with a salt-crystal ceiling; statues carved from salt (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept 'a café' (added near the entrance, not a feature of the underground rooms).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO things visitors are advised to do before they go.
parts.answer: wear comfortable shoes; bring a light jacket (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Why is the mine a popular place to visit in summer?
parts.answer: it is cool all year round
parts.working: Accept 'it is cool underground'.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE details that the article gives about the mine's history or its visitors.
parts.answer: the salt was formed when an ancient sea dried up; the mine is one of the largest in the world; the walk back up the stairs is tiring; a café has been added (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of the four points in the answer. Accept only details stated in the text.

practice.stem:
Read the article about the revival of calligraphy among young people, and then answer the questions.

The return of the reed pen
In an age of keyboards and touchscreens, it might seem surprising that classes in Arabic and Urdu calligraphy are fully booked in cities such as Lahore, Karachi and Peshawar. Yet teachers report that the number of young students has risen sharply over the past five years.
Calligrapher Imran Siddiqui has taught for over twenty years in a studio near the old walled city of Lahore. He believes social media is partly responsible: short videos of artists forming beautiful letters with a single stroke have attracted millions of viewers. 'People see the videos and think it looks easy,' he smiles. 'Then they discover that a single letter can take weeks to master.'
Students begin with a pen cut from a dried reed, called a qalam, and ink made from soot and gum. Imran insists on these traditional materials for the first six months because, he says, they teach patience and control in a way that a modern felt pen cannot.
Many students say calligraphy helps them relax after long hours of study. Others enjoy feeling connected to their culture and history. A few have turned their hobby into income by designing wedding invitations, shop signs and logos.
Not all traditionalists welcome these changes. Some older calligraphers complain that young artists mix styles without understanding the rules behind them. Imran disagrees. 'An art that never changes,' he says, 'is an art that is dying.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: In which part of Lahore is Imran's studio?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO details about the materials students use at the start.
parts.answer: Any two: a pen cut from a dried reed (qalam); ink made from soot; ink made from gum
parts.working: 1 mark each, maximum 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Why does Imran insist on traditional materials?
parts.working: Accept either 'patience' or 'control'.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE reasons why young people enjoy calligraphy, according to the article.
parts.answer: 1. it helps them relax after studying 2. they feel connected to their culture and history 3. some earn income from it (wedding invitations, signs, logos)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not credit 'it looks easy in videos' (why people start, not why they enjoy it).

parts.label: e
parts.text: What do some older calligraphers complain about?
parts.answer: young artists mix styles without understanding the rules

practice.stem:
Read the article about protecting farms from elephants in Sri Lanka, and then answer the questions.

Fences that bite back
For farmers in parts of Sri Lanka, a single night can destroy a whole season's work. Wild elephants, searching for food, walk out of the forest and into rice fields and vegetable gardens, eating and trampling crops. Each year, conflicts between people and elephants lead to deaths on both sides.
Traditional methods of scaring elephants away, such as lighting fires, beating drums or setting off firecrackers, often work only for a short time, as elephants soon realise that the noise is harmless. Electric fences are more effective but expensive to build and maintain, and some elephants have learned to push trees onto them to break the wire.
One cheaper solution uses an animal elephants dislike: bees. Farmers hang beehives on a wire between posts around their fields. When an elephant touches the wire, the hives swing and the angry bees fly out. Elephants have sensitive skin around their eyes and inside their trunks, and they avoid being stung.
The fences bring extra benefits. Farmers can sell the honey, which provides income, and the bees pollinate nearby crops and fruit trees, increasing harvests.
The method is not perfect. In very dry years, bee colonies sometimes leave the hives, and the fences need regular checking. But in trial villages, the number of elephant visits has fallen by more than half, and farmers say they sleep better at night.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO ways in which elephants damage farms.
parts.answer: 1. they eat crops 2. they trample crops
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO traditional methods of scaring elephants.
parts.answer: Any two: lighting fires; beating drums; setting off firecrackers
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give TWO disadvantages of electric fences.
parts.answer: Any two: expensive to build; expensive to maintain; elephants push trees onto them to break the wire
parts.working: 1 mark each. 'Expensive to build and maintain' = 1 mark unless clearly split.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO extra benefits of beehive fences.
parts.answer: 1. farmers can sell the honey / extra income 2. bees pollinate crops and fruit trees / increase harvests
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Read the article about first-aid training for young people in Pakistan, and then answer the questions.

Ten minutes that save lives
When a man collapsed at a crowded bus stop in Rawalpindi last winter, the first person to reach him was a seventeen-year-old student, Hamza Iqbal. While others filmed on their phones, Hamza checked whether the man was breathing, asked a bystander to call an ambulance on 1122, and began pressing hard and fast on the centre of his chest. By the time paramedics arrived, the man's heart was beating again.
Hamza had learned these skills only a month earlier in a free two-hour course run by volunteers at his college. The organisers, a group of young doctors, believe that every secondary-school student should be trained. 'An ambulance in a busy city may take ten minutes to arrive,' says Dr Saima Rehman. 'What happens in those ten minutes can decide whether someone survives.'
The course covers what to do if someone is choking, bleeding heavily, burned or has stopped breathing. Students practise on plastic dummies and work in pairs to practise placing an unconscious person on their side.
The doctors say the biggest obstacle is not difficulty but fear. Many people worry that they might make things worse or be blamed if the person does not recover. The trainers stress that doing something is almost always better than doing nothing.
Since the scheme began, more than 12,000 students in eight cities have been trained, and the organisers now hope to add first aid to the school timetable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give THREE things Hamza did to help the man.
parts.answer: 1. checked whether he was breathing 2. asked a bystander to call an ambulance (1122) 3. pressed hard and fast on the centre of his chest
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Who runs the first-aid courses?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give THREE situations that the course covers, apart from someone who has stopped breathing.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO reasons why people are afraid to give first aid.
parts.answer: 1. they worry they might make things worse 2. they worry they might be blamed (if the person does not recover)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Read the article about an indoor vertical farm in Dubai, and then answer the questions.

Farming without fields
In a warehouse on the edge of Dubai, where summer temperatures outside reach 45 °C, rows of lettuce, rocket and basil grow in trays stacked twelve levels high. No sunlight reaches them, and there is no soil. This is a vertical farm, and it produces about three tonnes of leafy vegetables every day.
Instead of sunlight, the plants receive light from red and blue LED lamps, which give the warehouse a pink glow. Red and blue are the colours plants use most for growth. Their roots hang in water containing exactly the nutrients they need. Sensors monitor temperature, humidity and carbon dioxide twenty-four hours a day, and a computer adjusts them automatically.
Supporters point out several advantages. The farm uses about 95 % less water than growing the same crops in fields, which matters in one of the driest countries on earth. No pesticides are needed, because insects cannot get in. And because the farm is close to the city, vegetables reach supermarkets within hours, rather than being flown in from abroad.
Critics, however, note that the lamps and air-conditioning use huge amounts of electricity, and unless this comes from renewable sources such as solar power, the environmental benefits are reduced. Vertical farms are also expensive to build, and so far they can grow only certain crops profitably. Wheat, rice and potatoes, for example, need too much space and light.
The company plans to cover the warehouse roof with solar panels next year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Why are red and blue lamps used?
parts.answer: red and blue are the colours plants use most for growth
parts.working: Do not accept 'to give a pink glow'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give THREE things the sensors monitor.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give THREE advantages of the vertical farm, according to supporters.
parts.answer: 1. uses about 95 % less water 2. no pesticides needed (insects cannot get in) 3. vegetables reach supermarkets within hours / not flown from abroad
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give TWO criticisms of vertical farms.
parts.answer: Any two: lamps and air-conditioning use huge amounts of electricity; expensive to build; only certain crops can be grown profitably
parts.working: 1 mark each. Examples (wheat, rice, potatoes) alone do not score unless linked to limited crops.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a river clean-up team in Lahore, and then answer the questions.

The river that came back
For decades, the stretch of river that runs past a row of old mills in Lahore was known only for the smell and the rubbish. Last year, a volunteer team began cleaning it every Sunday, and the results have surprised almost everybody.
The team uses small boats with nets to collect plastic, and it has removed more than a hundred bags of waste in the first six months. Each bag is sorted, so that bottles, bags and metal can be sold to recycling companies. The money from these sales is used to buy better equipment.
The clean-up has also brought back birds that had almost disappeared from the area. Local schoolchildren now visit the banks to count the species they see, and their results are added to a shared record kept by the team.
However, the leader, Ayesha Rafiq, warns that the work will never be finished while factories and households continue to throw waste into the water. She has asked the local council to fund a rubbish collection service for the mill area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO ways in which the team collects and deals with the waste.
parts.answer: uses small boats with nets to collect plastic; sorts the bags; sells bottles, bags and metal to recycling companies (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'sorts it' as one method only if the other method is also given.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO results of the clean-up that surprised people.
parts.answer: birds that had almost disappeared have come back; the stretch of river has improved (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept 'the team collected rubbish' as a surprising result.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give TWO reasons why Ayesha Rafiq says the work will never be finished.
parts.answer: factories continue to throw waste into the water; households continue to throw waste into the water (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE things that the schoolchildren do or the team does with the money or the records.
parts.answer: schoolchildren count the species they see; their results are added to a shared record; money from sales buys better equipment; the team keeps a record (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept only points that are stated in the article.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a community orchestra in Quetta, and then answer the questions.

No auditions, just music
The Quetta Community Orchestra was formed by a retired music teacher, Hamid Baloch, who wanted anyone with an instrument to have a chance to play. There are no auditions, and the group welcomes beginners as well as experienced musicians.
Rehearsals take place on Thursday evenings in a hall that is lent free of charge by a school. The members are of all ages, from young students to people in their seventies. Some bring instruments from home, while others borrow the orchestra's own violins, flutes and drums, which are kept in a cupboard at the back of the hall.
The orchestra gives two public concerts every year. Hamid says that the second concert is always the best, because the players have had time to become confident. Tickets are free, but a donation box is placed near the door to help pay for sheet music and repairs.
The group has no sponsor and does not charge fees, so it depends on the generosity of the people who attend. When a new member joins, Hamid always asks them to bring a friend to the next rehearsal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO facts about the rehearsals.
parts.answer: held on Thursday evenings; in a hall lent free by a school (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO ways in which the orchestra gets its instruments.
parts.answer: players bring their own instruments from home; the orchestra lends its own violins, flutes and drums (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'borrow' only with the orchestra's own instruments.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What is the money from the donation box used for?
parts.working: Accept either. Do not accept 'the concerts'.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE things that show the orchestra welcomes new players.
parts.answer: no auditions; welcomes beginners; members of all ages; new members are asked to bring a friend; (members from young students to people in their seventies) (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each. The concerts are not a welcome measure, so do not award marks for them.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a family-run bakery in Multan, and then answer the questions.

The oven never sleeps
The bakery on the corner of a busy market street in Multan opens before dawn and closes only when the last tray of bread has sold. It is run by three brothers, who inherited the business from their father, and the recipes have hardly changed in forty years.
The bakery is famous for its sweet fruit rolls, which are made with dates and walnuts, and for a flat bread baked against the hot clay walls of the oven. The brothers say that they do not use machines to shape the dough, because the rolls would then taste different.
One brother, Nadeem, manages the accounts and the orders for the wedding parties in the area. Customers can now place orders by phone, but the brothers still prefer to take most orders in person, because it gives them a chance to talk about the bread.
The bakery is not open on Fridays, which the brothers say is a family rule rather than a religious one. Instead, they spend the day visiting their mother and cousins in the old city.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO ingredients or features of the sweet fruit rolls.
parts.answer: dates; walnuts (any two) / made by hand, not machine
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept 'sweet' alone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give ONE reason why the brothers do not use machines to shape the dough.
parts.working: 1 mark. The article gives only this reason: the rolls would taste different.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What do the brothers prefer to do when taking orders?
parts.answer: take most orders in person; to talk with customers about the bread (any two points)
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two points. Do not accept 'by phone' (customers can use it, but the brothers prefer in person).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE things the article says about the brothers' day off or their family life.
parts.answer: the bakery is closed on Fridays; closure is a family rule, not a religious rule; they spend the day visiting their mother and cousins; they inherited the business from their father (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three correct points about the brothers or their family, taken from the article.

practice.stem:
Read the article about an eco-tourism camp in the Murree hills, and then answer the questions.

Sleeping under the pines
The Pine Ridge camp in the hills above Murree offers twelve wooden cabins, but guests are asked to leave their cars at the bottom of the hill. Electricity is provided by solar panels, and water is collected from a spring that runs beside the path.
The owner, Rubina Tariq, says that she wanted visitors to notice the forest rather than the comforts of a hotel. Guests help to plant trees on the first morning and are given a short lesson on the birds that nest in the pines. Meals are cooked on a wood stove and use vegetables from a garden next to the kitchen.
The camp is not suitable for families with very young children, because the path is steep and there is no medical post nearby. It is open from April to October, when the hills are at their greenest. In winter, the cabins are closed so that the trees and animals can rest.
Rubina hopes to add a second camp higher in the hills, but she says she will only build it if the local villagers agree to share the profits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO ways in which the camp protects the environment.
parts.answer: solar panels provide electricity; cars are left at the bottom of the hill; water comes from a spring; food from a garden (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'vegetables from a garden' as an environmental point only with the reason given.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO reasons why the camp is not suitable for some guests.
parts.answer: the path is steep; there is no medical post nearby; (it is not suitable for families with very young children) (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give TWO things guests do during their stay.
parts.answer: help to plant trees on the first morning; learn about the birds that nest in the pines (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'eat meals cooked on a wood stove' only if the other point is given.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE details about when the camp is open and what happens in winter.
parts.answer: open from April to October; closed in winter; the cabins close so the trees and animals can rest; the hills are greenest in the open season (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'open from April to October' and 'closed in winter' as separate details.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a chess tournament for children in Hyderabad, and then answer the questions.

The quiet game
The chess tournament for children at the community hall in Hyderabad is not the noisiest event of the year, but many parents say it is the most exciting. Each player must sit silently while the clock runs, and the referee does not allow any help from spectators.
The organisers, who are volunteers from a local chess club, say that the tournament is about more than winning. Every child receives a score sheet after each game, and the organisers write a short note explaining one thing the player did well and one thing to try next time.
This year, the tournament added a special group for players under eight. Their games are shorter, and the organisers allow a parent to sit beside the table, though not to speak. One volunteer said the youngest players often surprised the adults with their patience.
The winners receive a trophy and a set of chess books, but the organisers say that most children simply want to play again. Several players have already asked when the next tournament will be held.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO rules that players must follow during a game.
parts.answer: sit silently while the clock runs; no help from spectators (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept 'the referee' as a rule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO things that each child receives from the organisers.
parts.answer: a score sheet after each game; a short note about something done well and something to try next time (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What is special about the group for players under eight?
parts.answer: games are shorter and a parent may sit beside the table
parts.working: Accept either detail. Do not accept 'the parent can help' because parents may not speak.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE details about the prizes or the reactions of players and parents.
parts.answer: winners receive a trophy; a set of chess books; most children want to play again; some have asked when the next tournament is (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'parents say it is the most exciting event' as a valid reaction if three are given.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a community water-testing project in Gilgit, and then answer the questions.

What is in the water?
At a small clinic in Gilgit, a group of volunteers has begun testing the water from local springs and streams. Many families have reported stomach illnesses in the past year, and the volunteers wanted to find out whether the water was the cause.
The testing uses simple kits that change colour when harmful bacteria are present. Volunteers collect samples in clean bottles, label each one with the date and the place, and then leave them at the clinic for two days before reading the results.
So far, the team has found that water from two springs near the main road is unsafe to drink. The local council has closed the springs and has promised to fix the pipes that carry water to the village, but the work will take several months.
In the meantime, the clinic is giving away boiling kits to families, and volunteers visit each home to show them how to boil water safely. The team says that boiling is effective, but it is also expensive in fuel, which is why the council is looking at cheaper alternatives.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO things the volunteers do with each water sample.
parts.answer: label it with the date and place; leave it at the clinic for two days (any two) / collect it in clean bottles
parts.working: 1 mark each. The kits are used to test; the bottles are used to collect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO reasons why the volunteers started testing the water.
parts.answer: many families had stomach illnesses in the past year; the volunteers wanted to know if the water was the cause (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'families reported illnesses' and 'to find the cause' as two points.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What has the council done about the two unsafe springs?
parts.working: Accept 'closed them'. Do not accept 'fixed the pipes' (promised, not done).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE details about the boiling kits, the visits or the cost of boiling.
parts.answer: kits are given away at the clinic; volunteers visit each home to show families how to boil water; boiling is expensive in fuel; the council is looking at cheaper alternatives (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept only details stated in the text.

practice.stem:
Read the article about a rooftop garden in Islamabad, and then answer the questions.

Vegetables above the traffic
On the roof of a block of flats in Islamabad, a group of neighbours has built a garden that now produces tomatoes, peas, mint and a few rows of potatoes. The project began two years ago, when the residents were looking for somewhere to grow food in a crowded area with no yard.
The soil was brought up in sacks by lift, and the residents built wooden beds to hold it. Because the roof is hot in summer, they put shade cloth over the beds and watered them early each morning. Rainwater from the roof is stored in barrels, which means the garden uses very little tap water.
Not every idea worked well. The first attempt at growing maize failed because the plants were blown over by the wind. The gardeners now grow only low crops in the windier corner, and they have planted a row of small trees to shelter the beds.
The produce is shared among the families who help with the work. Any surplus is sold at a weekend stall at the entrance of the flats, and the money buys seeds and compost for the next season.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give TWO things the residents used to build the garden.
parts.answer: soil in sacks; wooden beds; shade cloth; barrels for rainwater (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'the soil was carried up by lift' only with the soil stated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give TWO ways in which the garden saves water.
parts.answer: rainwater is stored in barrels; watering early each morning; shade cloth reduces evaporation; the garden uses very little tap water (any two)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Shade cloth is for heat, but accept it when linked to watering.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Why did the first maize crop fail?
parts.answer: the plants were blown over by the wind
parts.working: Accept 'wind'. Do not accept 'the roof was too hot' (not the cause given).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give THREE details about how the vegetables are used or sold.
parts.answer: shared among the families who help; surplus sold at a weekend stall; money buys seeds and compost; (produce is grown on the roof) (any three)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three correct details.

practice.subtopic: Matching to sections of one article
practice.stem:
Read the article about rooftop gardens in Karachi, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

Green roofs over a busy city

A
When Sadia Memon moved into a fourth-floor flat in Gulshan-e-Iqbal, the only outdoor space was a flat concrete roof that the building shared. In summer it became so hot that nobody went up there. Sadia asked her neighbours if she could put a few pots of mint and chillies in one corner. Most of them laughed, but nobody said no.

B
Within a year, the corner had become a small garden of tomatoes, coriander and a lemon tree in a large plastic drum. Sadia waters everything early in the morning with water left over from washing vegetables. 'Plants are not fussy about where their water comes from,' she says. She also puts a layer of dry leaves on the soil so that it does not dry out in the afternoon sun.

C
The biggest surprise was the effect on the flats below. Neighbours on the top floor noticed that their rooms felt cooler, and one family switched off their air conditioner for two hours a day. Engineers say that soil and leaves absorb heat that would otherwise pass straight through the concrete into the building.

D
Now eleven of the sixteen families in the building help with the garden, and children come up after school to pick tomatoes. Sadia runs a free workshop on the first Sunday of every month for anyone in the area who wants to start their own roof garden. Her advice is simple: 'Start with one pot. Plants teach you the rest.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which section describes how Sadia saves water?
parts.working: B: 'water left over from washing vegetables'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which section mentions a reaction from neighbours that was not very encouraging?
parts.working: A: 'Most of them laughed'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which section explains why the garden lowered the temperature indoors?
parts.working: C: soil and leaves absorb heat that would pass through the concrete.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which section says Sadia shares her knowledge with other people?
parts.working: D: free monthly workshop. Not B, which describes her methods but not teaching others.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which section describes what the roof was like before the garden?
parts.working: A: flat concrete roof, so hot nobody went up.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which section mentions a family using less electricity?
parts.working: C: switched off their air conditioner for two hours a day.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Which section gives a method of stopping the soil from losing moisture?
parts.working: B: a layer of dry leaves so the soil does not dry out.

practice.subtopic: Matching to sections of one article
practice.stem:
Read the article about adults learning to swim, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

Never too late to swim

A
Forty-two-year-old Farhan Ali grew up in a desert town where the nearest river was two hours away. 'There was nowhere to learn, so I never did,' he explains. When his own children started swimming lessons in Islamabad, he sat by the pool every Saturday, feeling embarrassed that he could not join them in the water.

B
Farhan's fear was not unusual. Swimming teachers say that adults often find it harder than children because they remember frightening moments, such as slipping under the water at a beach. Adults also tend to hold their breath and tense their muscles, which actually makes the body sink.

C
The adult class Farhan joined began with no swimming at all. For the first two lessons, the six learners simply stood in shallow water, blew bubbles and practised floating while holding the side. 'Our teacher told us that the water would hold us up if we let it,' Farhan says. By the fifth week he could swim a whole width.

D
Six months later, Farhan swam his first length alongside his daughter. He now goes to the pool twice a week before work and says it has helped his back pain more than any medicine. He has also persuaded two colleagues to sign up for the next beginners' course.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which section explains why Farhan did not learn to swim as a child?
parts.working: A: nowhere to learn; nearest river two hours away.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which section describes a health benefit Farhan has noticed?
parts.working: D: helped his back pain.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which section mentions a habit that makes swimming more difficult for adults?
parts.working: B: holding their breath and tensing muscles makes the body sink.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which section describes the first activities in Farhan's class?
parts.working: C: standing in shallow water, blowing bubbles, floating.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which section says Farhan encouraged other people to learn?
parts.working: D: persuaded two colleagues to sign up.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which section describes how Farhan felt while watching his children?
parts.working: A: embarrassed.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Which section says how many people were learning in Farhan's class?
parts.working: C: the six learners.

practice.subtopic: Matching to sections of one article
practice.stem:
Read the article about a school astronomy club in northern Pakistan, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

Stargazing in the mountains

A
The astronomy club at a secondary school near Gilgit started with one second-hand telescope, bought by a physics teacher with money from a school cake sale. On the first evening, only four students came. Now more than thirty meet on the school's playing field on clear nights.

B
Members say the mountains are one of the best places in the country to look at the sky. There are very few street lights, and the air is dry and clean, especially in winter. 'In Lahore I could see maybe twenty stars,' says Hina, who moved to Gilgit two years ago. 'Here I can see the Milky Way with my own eyes.'

C
Watching the sky is not always comfortable. In January the temperature at night can fall well below zero, so students bring thick blankets and flasks of hot tea. They have also learned to use red torches, because white light makes it harder for their eyes to adjust to the dark.

D
Last year the club photographed the Moon through the telescope using a mobile phone, and the pictures were shown at a national science festival. The students now hope to raise money for a larger telescope so that they can see the rings of Saturn more clearly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which section says the club's work was seen by people across the country?
parts.working: D: pictures shown at a national science festival.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which section explains how the club got its first equipment?
parts.working: A: teacher bought it with cake-sale money.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which section compares the night sky in two different places?
parts.working: B: Hina compares Lahore and Gilgit.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which section mentions a piece of equipment that protects the students' night vision?
parts.working: C: red torches.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which section describes how the club has grown?
parts.working: A: four students at first, now more than thirty.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which section gives the club's plan for the future?
parts.working: D: raise money for a larger telescope.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Which section mentions a difficulty caused by the weather?
parts.working: C: temperature well below zero in January.

practice.subtopic: Matching to sections of one article
practice.stem:
Read the article about a school recycling project, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

From bottles to benches

A
Students at a girls' school in Faisalabad noticed that the bins outside their canteen were full of plastic water bottles every afternoon. Their science teacher challenged them to find a use for the bottles instead of sending them to the city rubbish dump.

B
After reading about similar projects online, the students decided to make 'eco-bricks': empty bottles packed tightly with clean plastic wrappers until they are as hard as wood. Each brick took about twenty minutes to fill. Families helped by saving wrappers at home and sending them to school in bags.

C
It took four months to make 600 bricks. A local builder offered to help for free, and showed the students how to join the bricks together with a mixture of clay and straw. The finished result was two long benches in the shade of the school's neem tree.

D
The benches are now the most popular place to sit at break time. The project has also changed habits: many students now bring metal water bottles from home, and the canteen has started selling drinks in glasses that are washed and reused.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which section describes how the project changed what students drink from?
parts.working: D: metal water bottles from home.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which section explains what an eco-brick is?
parts.working: B: bottle packed tightly with clean plastic wrappers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which section mentions a professional who gave help without payment?
parts.working: C: a local builder helped for free. Not B: families helped but are not professionals.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which section says where the idea for the project first came from?
parts.working: A: the science teacher's challenge after students noticed full bins.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which section gives the total number of bricks made?
parts.working: C: 600 bricks.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which section describes a change made by the canteen?
parts.working: D: drinks sold in reusable glasses.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Which section mentions how long it took to make one brick?
parts.working: B: about twenty minutes each.

practice.subtopic: Matching to sections of one article
practice.stem:
Read the article about volunteers who protect sea turtles near Karachi, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

Night shift on the beach

A
Every year, from about August to December, female green turtles come out of the Arabian Sea at night to lay their eggs on the sandy beaches west of Karachi. Each turtle digs a hole with her back flippers, lays around a hundred eggs, covers them with sand and returns to the sea before sunrise.

B
Nineteen-year-old Ayesha has volunteered with a turtle protection group for three seasons. Her job is to walk the beach between midnight and four in the morning with a dim torch and a notebook. When she finds a nest, she records the time and the exact place so that it can be watched.

C
The eggs face many dangers. Stray dogs dig them up, and bright lights from beach huts can confuse baby turtles when they hatch, so they crawl towards the land instead of the sea. Volunteers sometimes move eggs to a fenced area of the beach where they are safe.

D
For Ayesha, the best moment is watching the babies hatch about two months later. 'They are smaller than my hand, and they run straight for the waves,' she says. 'Only a few will survive to become adults, but every one we help gives the species a better chance.'

Cooking with the sun

Last spring, the women's group in Bhitai village received six solar cookers from a charity. Most families had never heard of cooking without firewood. Nasreen Bibi, the group's leader, was the first to try one, and she admits that her first attempt at chapatis was a disaster.

A solar cooker is a metal box lined with mirrors. It has a glass lid that lets sunlight in and traps the heat. Food takes longer to cook than on a gas stove, so the women plan their meals in the morning. Rice needs about two hours, but it tastes better because it cooks slowly.

The most noticeable benefit is the saving in firewood. Before the project, families walked up to three kilometres every few days to collect wood. Now the cookers use only sunlight, and several households have stopped cutting down the small trees near the village.

Why teenagers can't get up

A
Parents often complain that teenagers stay up too late and are impossible to wake in the morning. Many assume this is simply laziness or too much time on phones. Scientists who study sleep, however, say the truth is more complicated, and that the teenage brain really does work on a different timetable.

B
During adolescence, the body begins to release melatonin, the hormone that makes us feel sleepy, about two hours later in the evening than it did in childhood. A fourteen-year-old who tries to sleep at nine o'clock may simply lie awake. Yet teenagers still need roughly eight to ten hours of sleep a night, so an early start leaves many of them short of rest.

C
The effects of this lost sleep are not small. Tired students find it harder to concentrate and remember new information, and they are more likely to feel irritable or low. Some studies have also linked a lack of sleep to more accidents among young drivers and cyclists.

D
A few schools have experimented with starting lessons later, and several reported better attendance and fewer students falling asleep in class. Not everyone is convinced: later finishing times can clash with sports practice and part-time jobs. Experts agree, though, that teenagers themselves can help by keeping screens out of the bedroom and getting morning daylight.

Watching the ghost of the mountains

A
Snow leopards are among the hardest big cats in the world to study. They live on steep, rocky slopes high in the mountains of Central and South Asia, they are mostly active at dawn and dusk, and their grey, spotted coats blend perfectly into the rocks. Many local herders have lived in snow leopard country all their lives without ever seeing one.

B
To learn about them, researchers in northern Pakistan use camera traps: small cameras fixed to rocks that take a photograph whenever an animal walks past. Because every snow leopard has a unique pattern of spots, scientists can identify individual cats from the pictures and estimate how many live in an area.

C
The work depends on local people. Herders often know the paths that wild animals use, and they guide researchers to the best places for cameras. In return, some conservation groups help villages to build stronger animal pens, so that leopards cannot kill sheep and goats at night. This has reduced the number of leopards killed by angry farmers.

D
The photographs have produced some surprises, including images of a mother with three cubs in a valley where no snow leopards had been recorded for years. Researchers warn, though, that warmer temperatures could push the cats' prey higher up the mountains, leaving less space for both.

A sitar lesson across the ocean

Online lessons have obvious limits. When the internet connection is slow, the sound reaches Zara a second late, which makes playing together impossible. Her teacher cannot reach over and move her fingers into the correct position, so he has to describe exactly what he wants. 'At first I found that frustrating,' Zara admits, 'but now I listen far more carefully.'

There are advantages, too. Each lesson is recorded, so Zara can watch difficult passages again during the week. Ustad Rashid also teaches students in Dubai, Manchester and Karachi, and once a term they all join one video call to perform for each other. 'It feels like a little international family,' he says.

Zara's parents first suggested the sitar because they wanted her to stay connected to the music her grandparents loved. She was not keen at first, preferring the guitar. Tiny forests, big difference

A
On a strip of wasteland beside a motorway in Lahore, where rubbish used to pile up, there is now a dense thicket of trees taller than a person. It was planted less than three years ago using a method developed by a Japanese botanist, Akira Miyawaki, in which dozens of native species are planted very close together.

B
Because the young trees are so crowded, they compete for light and grow upwards quickly. Supporters say these 'tiny forests' can become established in a few years, rather than the decades a normal woodland needs. After the first two or three years of watering and weeding, they are expected to look after themselves.

C
City planners are interested because trees cool the air around them. On summer afternoons, paved streets and buildings in large cities can be several degrees hotter than the surrounding countryside, an effect known as the 'urban heat island'. Shade and water released from leaves both help to lower the temperature.

D
Critics point out that tiny forests are expensive to plant, because of the large number of saplings and the preparation of the soil. Others worry that too many fast-growing trees in a small space may not all survive. Supporters reply that even if some die, the forest as a whole still provides shelter for birds and insects in places where there was nothing before.

The museum of ordinary things

A
Most museums display treasures: gold jewellery, ancient swords, paintings by famous artists. A small museum in Peshawar does the opposite. Its glass cases hold a broken transistor radio, a school satchel from the 1970s, a set of tin cups and a bicycle bell. The founder, retired schoolteacher Gul Rehman, calls it 'a museum of everyday life'.

B
Gul began collecting thirty years ago, when he noticed that his neighbours were throwing away things their parents had used for decades. 'Nobody thought these objects mattered,' he says. 'But once they are gone, our grandchildren will have no idea how we lived.' Every item has a label explaining who owned it and how it was used.

C
Visitors react in surprising ways. Older people often stand in front of a cabinet for a long time, then start telling strangers about their own childhood. Gul now records these stories on his phone and has collected more than two hundred of them. Young visitors, meanwhile, are amazed that people once listened to cricket matches on the radio instead of watching them.

D
The museum survives on donations, and the building badly needs a new roof before the next monsoon. A university in the city has offered to help digitise the collection and the recorded stories, so that people around the world can explore them online. Gul is pleased, but insists that 'nothing replaces holding the real thing in your hands.'

Ali Raza started keeping bees in Gilgit when his father's apricot orchard began producing less fruit. He had no experience and learned from a video his cousin sent from Turkey. His first hive was built from old crates, and it attracted more wasps than honeybees.

B
The hardest season is winter. The bees must survive for months in the cold without flowers. Ali wraps each hive in blankets and leaves a store of honey inside. He opens the hives only once a month, because disturbing them in cold air can kill the colony.

C
Ali sells his honey at the Sunday market, where tourists often buy it. However, a wholesaler offered him a price that was too low, so he now sells most of his honey directly to hotels. He says the honey tastes different each season, depending on which flowers are in bloom.

D
Ali is training ten young men from nearby villages, and they now keep their own hives. He believes beekeeping could strengthen the local economy, but he warns that buying too many hives can spread disease. His goal is to create a beekeepers' cooperative within three years.

The robot that carries the medicine

At the Maasstad Hospital in Rotterdam, a small white robot travels through the corridors all day. It carries blood samples, medicines and clean linen between the wards and the laboratory. Staff say it has changed the rhythm of the morning, because nurses no longer leave their patients to fetch supplies.

The robot was first tested in one ward only. Engineers had to teach it to wait politely when a door is closed, and to avoid trolleys that are left in the way. Early versions sometimes stopped in the middle of a corridor. Today it can find its own route, but a porter still rides with it up the lift.
