Some nurses were worried that the machine would make their job more stressful. However, the staff who use it most say that the robot sends a message when it arrives, which means they can plan their work better. Patients have also noticed that medicines arrive on time, even on busy nights.

The hospital plans to buy six more robots, but only if it can afford the cost of their maintenance. Managers are also considering a version that can carry heavier loads. An administrator has pointed out that the real test will be whether the robots still help when the building is at its busiest.

The Hazara Community Kitchen opened in an old printing press on Jinnah Road. It serves a hot meal to anyone who arrives before two o'clock, and nobody is asked to pay. The founder, Shabana Akhtar, used to run a catering business, but she wanted to feed people who could not afford a restaurant.

Read the article about saving water at home, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

Every drop counts

A
In many cities, people only think about water when the taps run dry. Yet engineers warn that demand is growing faster than supply in much of South Asia, as populations rise and underground water levels fall. In some neighbourhoods, families already depend on water tankers for part of the year, paying far more per litre than those connected to the mains.

B
The good news, according to researchers who measured water use in two hundred homes, is that households waste far more than they realise. A single dripping tap can lose thousands of litres a year, and a leaking toilet cistern even more, often silently. 'Most families we visited had no idea they had a leak,' said one of the team. Simple repairs cost very little compared with the water saved.

C
Habits matter too, although changing them is harder. Washing a car with a bucket instead of a hose, or turning off the tap while brushing teeth, may seem trivial. But the researchers found that when families saw a weekly chart of their own water use, many cut their consumption without being asked, apparently motivated by comparing themselves with their neighbours.

D
Some experts argue that individual efforts, while welcome, cannot solve the problem on their own. Agriculture uses by far the largest share of water in the region, and old city pipes lose a large proportion of their supply before it reaches anyone's home. Real progress, they say, will need investment by governments as well as care from citizens.

Breathing room

A
As a child in Quetta, Mahnoor Baloch was the girl who sat on the bench during sports lessons. Cold, dry air brought on her asthma attacks, and her teachers, worried about her safety, rarely let her run. 'Everyone was very kind,' she remembers, 'but kindness can also keep you very small.'

B
Things changed when she was fifteen and saw a new doctor, who adjusted her medicine and explained that, for most people, asthma that is well controlled need not stop them exercising. He suggested she start with short, gentle runs and always warm up slowly. Mahnoor was sceptical. 'I'd spent ten years being told the opposite,' she says.

C
The early months were discouraging. She could barely jog for five minutes, and on windy days she had to stop completely. She kept a diary of every run, noting the weather and how her breathing felt, and gradually noticed patterns: early mornings in winter were the worst, while warm, humid evenings were easiest.

D
Eight years later, Mahnoor has completed three marathons and now coaches a running group for teenagers with breathing conditions. She is careful not to promise too much. 'Asthma is different for everyone,' she tells them, 'and you must work with your doctor. But don't let other people decide what your body can do.'

Gardeners under the sea

A
Coral reefs cover a tiny fraction of the ocean floor, yet they shelter roughly a quarter of all marine species. In the Maldives, a nation of low-lying islands, reefs also act as natural sea walls, breaking up waves before they reach the shore. Fishing and tourism, the country's two biggest industries, both depend on healthy reefs.

B
When sea temperatures stay unusually high for several weeks, corals expel the tiny algae living inside them, which give them both their colour and most of their food. The corals turn white, a process called bleaching. If the water cools in time, they can recover; if not, they starve and die.

C
On one island, marine biologist Aminath Shareef leads a team that grows young corals on metal frames in the lagoon. Small fragments broken from healthy corals are tied to the frames, where they grow for a year or two before being attached to damaged parts of the reef. Hotel guests can sponsor a frame and receive photographs of its progress.

D
Aminath is honest about the limits of her work. 'We can restore a few football pitches of reef,' she says, 'but the oceans are warming over millions of square kilometres. If we don't reduce emissions, we are only buying time.' Even so, she believes the frames help train a new generation of local divers who care about the sea.

practice.subtopic: Matching to sections of one article
practice.stem:
Read the article about why people hate waiting, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

The science of the queue

A
Whether at a bank, a petrol station or a hospital, most of us spend many hours of our lives waiting in line. Psychologists who study queues have found something curious: how annoyed we feel often has little to do with how long we actually wait. A ten-minute wait can feel unbearable in one situation and perfectly acceptable in another.

B
One reason is uncertainty. People become much more anxious when they do not know how long a wait will last. This is why some airports and theme parks display estimated waiting times, and why many people prefer a slow queue that moves steadily to a fast one that keeps stopping. Unexplained delays are tolerated far less than those whose cause is known.

C
Fairness matters even more. Customers become angry if someone who arrived later is served first, even if their own wait is not affected. For this reason, some banks have replaced several separate lines with a single queue that feeds all the counters. Each person may not be served any faster, but nobody can feel that they chose the wrong line.

D
Businesses have also discovered that occupied time feels shorter than empty time. Mirrors beside lifts, music on telephone lines and television screens in waiting rooms are all designed to distract us. Critics argue that these tricks simply hide poor service, and that the real solution is to employ more staff. The psychologists' reply is that both approaches have a place.

Seven days offline

A
When the head teacher of a boarding school in Murree announced that students would hand in their phones for a whole week, the reaction was close to panic. Several parents emailed to object, arguing that they needed to contact their children. The school agreed that a landline in the office would be available every evening, and the experiment went ahead.

B
The first two days were difficult. Students described feeling restless and repeatedly reaching into empty pockets. 'I kept thinking I was missing something important,' said one Year 11 boy. Teachers noticed that conversations at meals were awkward at first, as if students had forgotten how to talk without a screen to look at.

C
By midweek, the mood had changed. The library, usually quiet, was full in the evenings, and a group of girls organised a chess tournament that attracted sixty players. Many students reported falling asleep earlier and waking up feeling more refreshed. Some admitted, slightly reluctantly, that they had enjoyed the week more than they expected.

D
Not everyone was won over. A few students argued that phones were essential for schoolwork, and that the week had simply made revision harder. Others pointed out that a single week proved very little, since everyone knew their phones would come back. The school now plans one phone-free evening every week, a compromise that most students seem willing to accept.

Younger women have joined in recent years, although most of them learned to use computers before they learned to weave. The eldest weaver, who is ninety-one, says she is proud that her designs will continue, but she worries that people no longer have the patience to sit at a loom for hours.

Swapping words over tea

A
On Thursday evenings, the back room of a small café in Kadıköy is filled with people who want to practise a language. Tables are marked with flags, and a bowl of sugar cubes is placed in the centre. Every participant must speak only the language they are practising for at least half an hour.

B
The café was founded by a former teacher who noticed that students in her evening classes never spoke outside the classroom. She set up the exchange to give learners a relaxed setting. Nobody is graded, and mistakes are corrected with a smile, not a red pen.

C
Some regulars say the most useful part is not grammar but slang, which textbooks rarely teach. One engineer from Ankara said he finally understood the jokes his colleagues had been making. Others come simply to meet new people, and several friendships have lasted for years.

D
The organiser has recently been asked to run similar meetings in other cities, but she is cautious. She believes that the success of the evening depends on the atmosphere of the café and on its regular volunteers, who greet newcomers. She would prefer to grow slowly rather than lose that warmth.

Read the article about a community-owned cinema in a Scottish town, in which four sections are labelled A–D, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once.

Reels run by the village

A
The Balloch Picture House closed in 2009 after its owners retired, and for a decade the building stood empty. When the last local cinema was sold for housing, residents formed a trust and asked the community to buy shares. Within eighteen months they had raised enough to reopen the building.

B
The volunteers have had to learn skills that none of them had before, from projecting digital films to repairing the old wooden seats. A retired electrician now spends every Tuesday rewiring the lights, while a teacher runs a film club for teenagers. The cinema now shows three films a week.

C
Critics once argued that a small town could never support a cinema, especially when the nearest multiplex is only fifteen minutes away by car. The trust counters that the audience is loyal: local people come to see films they would otherwise miss, and they often stay afterwards to discuss them in the café.

D
Next year the trust hopes to install a second screen for children's films, but this depends on a grant that has not yet been approved. Some members think the project is too ambitious, while others say that a town which has lost its cinema once should not take the risk of losing it again.

practice.stem:

Second chances at the kennels

A
Most dogs arrive at the Lahore Animal Care Centre thin, frightened, or with injuries from traffic. The staff take in roughly forty animals a month, and they try to keep every new arrival in a quiet pen for a week before anyone tries to touch them. Patience, the centre's founder says, is more useful than any medicine.

B
Adoption is not automatic. Families must attend two interviews, and the centre sends a volunteer to their home. This can seem strict, but the staff have seen too many dogs returned after impulsive adoptions. Those who pass the checks receive a free bag of food and a training voucher.

C
Not every dog is suitable for a family. Some animals remain at the centre for more than a year, because they react badly to children or to other dogs. The team does not give up on them. Instead, they arrange long walks and training sessions that help the dogs feel calmer.

D
The centre is facing a shortage of money because donations fell after last year's floods. The founder says that a single kennel repair costs more than a month's food. She has started a monthly subscription scheme, although she admits that many former supporters have not yet signed up.

My first job

A  Hamza, 17
I help in my uncle's mobile phone shop in Rawalpindi on Saturdays. Mostly I put protective screens on phones and explain prices to customers. At first I was too shy to speak to adults, but now I enjoy it. The pay is small, but my uncle gives me a bonus if the shop has a good month.

B  Mariam, 16
I tutor two younger girls in maths after school, three evenings a week. Explaining fractions to a nine-year-old is much harder than doing them myself! I'm saving everything I earn for a laptop, and I've already reached half the price. The best part is when something suddenly makes sense to them.

C  Daniel, 17
I deliver newspapers in my town in England before school. I have to get up at half past five, which is terrible in winter when it's dark and raining. But I'm paid every Friday, and cycling the route has made me much fitter. I've learned to plan my time better because I can't be late for school.

D  Sana, 16
I work at a bakery counter in Karachi during the school holidays. On my first day I dropped a whole tray of cupcakes, and I nearly cried. The owner just laughed and said everyone does it once. Now I'm trusted with the till, and I'm learning to decorate cakes, which I'd like to do as a career.

I take the Metro bus to college every day. It's air-conditioned, which makes a huge difference in June, and it's much cheaper than a rickshaw. The only problem is that it's very crowded at eight o'clock, so I usually have to stand for the whole journey.

B  Leila, Amsterdam
Like most people here, I cycle to work. There are separate bike lanes almost everywhere, so I feel safe. It takes twenty minutes and I arrive feeling awake. When there's ice on the roads in winter, though, I sometimes take the tram instead.

My father drops me at school on his motorbike on his way to the office. I like it because we talk on the way, and it's the only time we spend alone together on weekdays. On rainy days we both arrive soaking wet, so I keep spare socks in my bag!

D  Kenji, Tokyo
I walk ten minutes to the station and then take two trains. The trains are always exactly on time, so I can plan my morning to the minute. I use the journey to read or study vocabulary. It's long — about an hour each way — but I don't mind.

I joined an online coding course for beginners and made a simple game where a cat catches falling fish. It took me three weeks. My younger brother plays it all the time, which is the best compliment. Next I want to learn to make phone apps.

I tried rock climbing at an indoor wall near my home in Wales. I was scared of heights, so the first time I only got halfway up before asking to come down. By the end of the holiday I'd reached the top of the hardest wall for beginners. It's taught me that fear isn't a reason to stop.

Walking through streets that people built over four thousand years ago was amazing. Our guide showed us the drains and the Great Bath, and explained how carefully the city was planned. It was extremely hot, though, and I wish we had gone in winter instead of April.

My favourite part was a room where you could make your hair stand on end using static electricity. Everything was hands-on, so even students who normally find science boring were busy. I've persuaded my parents to take my little sister there.

This was a three-day camping trip, the first time I had slept in a tent. The views of Nanga Parbat in the early morning were unforgettable. The walk up was really tiring and my boots gave me blisters, but the teachers made sure nobody was left behind.

Where we stayed

A  River View Lodge
The rooms were simple but very clean, and we fell asleep to the sound of the river. Breakfast was the highlight: fresh trout and hot parathas. The only disappointment was the Wi-Fi, which only worked in the reception area.

B  Apple Tree Guesthouse
A family-run place in the middle of an orchard. The owner's children showed our kids how to pick apples, and they still talk about it. It is a long walk from the main road, so it is not ideal if you have heavy luggage.

C  Snowline Hotel
Comfortable beds, hot water all the time and heating that actually works — important in December! It's more expensive than other places nearby, but we felt it was worth it. Staff booked a jeep for us to visit Malam Jabba.

D  Green Valley Rest House
The cheapest place we found, and good value. The building is old and the bathroom was a bit small, but the manager was incredibly helpful and gave us a hand-drawn map of local walking routes. We'd happily stay again.

I went to Turkey with my sister when I was twenty-five, and we planned every hour. We visited eight cities in two weeks. It was exhausting, but I came home with hundreds of photos and a much better sense of history.

Young scientists

A  Ahmed
I tested whether the colour of a roof affects the temperature inside a model house. I built four identical cardboard houses and painted the roofs white, red, green and black, then left them in the sun with thermometers inside. The white one stayed coolest by several degrees. B  Mehwish
My project was about filtering muddy water using sand, gravel and charcoal in a plastic bottle. The water came out clear, but my teacher pointed out that clear water isn't necessarily safe to drink, because germs are invisible. That was an important lesson, and I added boiling as a final step in my display.

C  Rohan
I compared how fast cress seeds grew when watered with tap water, rainwater and water that had been used to wash rice. I expected the rice water to win because it contains starch, but there was almost no difference. I was disappointed at first, but the judges said an unexpected result is still a valid result.

D  Aisha
I built a simple alarm that sounds when a water tank is about to overflow, using two wires, a battery and a buzzer. When the water touches both wires, it completes the circuit. It cost less than five hundred rupees. Our neighbour has already asked me to make one for him.

Starting again abroad

A  Saima, from Multan to Toronto
The cold was the first shock. I had never seen snow, and in my first winter I didn't own proper boots. What helped most was a neighbour, an elderly woman from Portugal, who invited us for dinner in our first week. Her kindness made me feel I could belong here.

B  Javier, from Mexico to Dubai
I came for a job in engineering. Work was easy to adjust to, because everyone spoke English in the office, but it took me a long time to make friends outside work. Joining a weekend football team changed that. Now I have friends from about ten different countries.

C  Usman, from Peshawar to Berlin
Learning German was much harder than I imagined. For months I avoided phoning anyone because I was afraid of making mistakes. In the end I found a language exchange partner: I help her with Urdu and she helps me with German. Mistakes don't embarrass me any more.

D  Grace, from Nigeria to Lahore
I moved here to study medicine. People warned me I might feel isolated, but the opposite happened — classmates invited me to weddings and taught me to cook daal. The thing I still miss is my mother's cooking, especially jollof rice, which I can't make as well as she does.

I'm in charge of collecting unsold bread and fruit from shops at closing time. Before we started, most of it was thrown away. The hardest part is persuading shop owners that the food will be handled safely — some still refuse — but the number of shops taking part has doubled this year.

C  Mrs Perveen
I'm seventy-one, and I peel vegetables every morning with three other women my age. People think we are helping others, but honestly the kitchen helps us too. Since my husband died, it has given me a reason to get up and a group of friends to talk to.

D  Ben

Training secrets

A  Shahid, squash player
People imagine squash is all about hitting the ball hard, but most of my training is footwork. I spend an hour a day on 'ghosting' — moving around the court without a ball, practising the steps. My coach says that if your feet are in the right place, the shot is easy.

B  Elena, swimmer
I train in the pool at five in the morning, six days a week. But the part people don't see is sleep. I'm in bed by nine every night, even at weekends. My friends think I'm boring, but without enough rest my times get slower and I pick up colds.

C  Rizwan, cricketer (fast bowler)
Fast bowling puts huge stress on the back, so I do a lot of strength work in the gym, especially for my core muscles. I also video my bowling action every week and compare it with older videos, because tiny changes can lead to injury.

D  Amna, long-distance runner
I used to run hard every day and kept getting injured. Now I follow a plan where most of my runs are slow and easy, with only two hard sessions a week. It felt strange to slow down to get faster, but my race times have improved a lot since I changed.

Learning a language later in life

A  Naveed, learning Chinese
I started Mandarin at thirty-five because my company trades with Chinese suppliers. The tones were a nightmare: the same sound can mean 'mother' or 'horse' depending on how you say it. What finally worked was singing along to Chinese pop songs in the car, which trained my ear.

B  Claire, learning Urdu
I married into a Pakistani family and wanted to talk to my mother-in-law, who speaks little English. I took a formal course, but I learned far more at family dinners, where nobody would translate for me. Now we chat on the phone every week, which means a lot to both of us.

C  Tariq, learning French
I'm a retired teacher and learning French purely for pleasure. I use an app for fifteen minutes every day; I've kept going for over four hundred days without a break. I'm still nervous about speaking, though, so next year I'm going on a two-week course in France to push myself.

D  Mei, learning Arabic
I studied Arabic at university, then forgot most of it during ten years of not using it. When I moved to Jordan for work, it came back surprisingly quickly. I think the words were still somewhere in my memory, waiting. I'd tell anyone: nothing you learn is ever completely wasted.

When the words won't come

A  Sameer, novelist
I don't really believe in 'writer's block'. Plumbers don't get plumber's block. When I'm stuck, it's usually because I'm trying to write the perfect sentence, so I give myself permission to write badly. A terrible page can be fixed; an empty one can't.

B  Hannah, poet
For me, the silence is part of the process. I might write nothing for two months and then three poems in a week. I used to panic during those gaps, but I've learned they're when ideas are quietly forming. I read a lot and go for long walks, and I try not to force anything.

C  Farah, journalist
In journalism you can't wait for inspiration — the deadline is at six o'clock whether you feel creative or not. So I rely on structure: I start with the facts, then the quotes, and only then worry about style. Having a routine takes the pressure off feeling inspired.

D  Osman, screenwriter
When I'm stuck, I talk the story through with my sister, who isn't a writer at all. Explaining it to her forces me to see where the plot doesn't make sense. Half the time she doesn't even need to say anything — just having someone listen helps me find the answer.

A  Ghulam Hussain, Sindh
The heat in May now comes earlier and stays longer, and my wheat used to ripen before it was fully grown. Two years ago I switched to a variety that matures faster, and I sow a couple of weeks earlier. The harvest is a little smaller, but at least it is reliable.

B  Rukhsana Bibi, Punjab
Our canal water arrives less often than it did when my father farmed, so every drop matters. We have levelled our fields with a laser so that water spreads evenly instead of collecting in low corners. It was expensive, and I was against it at first, but we now use far less water for the same crop.

C  Maria Santos, Brazil
Instead of clearing all the trees, I grow coffee under the shade of taller trees. Coffee plants hate extreme heat, and the shade keeps them cooler. The trees also hold the soil together in heavy rain. My neighbours thought I was old-fashioned, but now some are copying me.

D  Arif Khan, Gilgit-Baltistan
Our streams depend on melting glaciers. For now there is more water than ever in summer, as the ice melts faster, but the old people warn that one day it could suddenly decrease. We are building small stone tanks to store water, and some families are planting cherries, which sell for good prices in the cities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which farmer accepted a lower yield in return for greater security?
parts.working: A: harvest smaller but reliable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which farmer was initially opposed to a change that proved successful?
parts.working: B: was against laser levelling at first.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which farmer describes a short-term benefit that may hide a long-term risk?
parts.working: D: more water now, but it could suddenly decrease.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which farmer uses a method that others first considered outdated?
parts.working: C: neighbours thought she was old-fashioned.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which farmer mentions a change that protects against erosion?
parts.working: C: trees hold the soil together in heavy rain.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which farmer has changed the timing of their work?
parts.working: A: sows a couple of weeks earlier.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Which farmer is preparing to store a resource for the future?
parts.working: D: building stone tanks.

parts.label: h
parts.text: Which farmer compares conditions now with those in a previous generation?
parts.working: B: canal water arrives less often than when her father farmed. D refers to old people's warnings about the future, not a comparison.

parts.label: i
parts.text: Which farmer is moving into a crop for its commercial value?
parts.working: D: cherries sell for good prices in cities.

practice.subtopic: Matching to four texts or sections (A–D)
practice.stem:
Read what four designers say about their plans for a new public library, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

Designing tomorrow's library

A  Saira, architect
Libraries used to be built like temples, with grand steps and heavy doors that said 'be quiet and behave'. I want the entrance to feel like a shop on a busy street: glass walls, so people passing can see children reading and families chatting inside. If people can't see in, many will never come in.

B  Matteo, interior designer
Not every visitor wants the same thing. Some need silence to study; others want to talk, play games or use computers. I'd divide the building into zones, with the noisiest areas near the entrance and the quietest at the top, so the sound naturally fades as you go higher.

C  Bushra, engineer
In our climate, the biggest cost of any public building is cooling. I'd use thick walls, small windows on the sunny side and a central courtyard with plants and a water feature, as traditional houses did. Some people call these ideas old-fashioned, but they cut electricity bills dramatically.

D  Jonas, librarian
Everyone is excited about technology, but I'd warn against filling the building with screens that will be out of date in five years. The most important thing a library offers is free space where anyone can stay as long as they like without buying anything. That, not gadgets, is what we must protect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which designer believes that visibility will attract new users?
parts.working: A: glass walls so passers-by can see in.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which designer is cautious about a popular trend?
parts.working: D: warns against filling the building with screens.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which designer defends ideas from the past against criticism?
parts.working: C: traditional techniques called old-fashioned but cut bills.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which designer organises space according to different needs?
parts.working: B: zones for silence and noise.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which designer criticises the message given by traditional library buildings?
parts.working: A: grand steps and heavy doors said 'be quiet and behave'.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which designer considers the long-term running costs of the building?
parts.working: C: cooling is the biggest cost.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Which designer emphasises that using a library should cost nothing?
parts.working: D: stay without buying anything.

parts.label: h
parts.text: Which designer uses the building's height to solve a problem?
parts.working: B: quietest areas at the top, sound fades.

practice.subtopic: Matching to four texts or sections (A–D)
practice.stem:
Read what four people say about homework, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once, and every letter is used at least once.

Is homework worth it?

A  Mr Asghar, maths teacher
In maths, practice is everything. A student can follow an example in class and still be unable to do the next question alone. Homework shows me who has really understood. That said, I'd rather set ten well-chosen questions than forty repetitive ones.

B  Mrs Lodhi, parent
My son spends three hours a night on homework and still has tuition at weekends. He hasn't played outside in months. I'm not against homework, but when it takes over a child's entire life, something has gone wrong. Schools need to talk to each other about how much they set.

C  Dr Rahman, education researcher
The evidence is mixed. For secondary students, moderate amounts of homework are linked to better results, but beyond a certain point the benefit disappears. For young children, there's very little evidence that it helps academically, although reading with parents clearly does.

D  Sara, Year 10 student
Honestly, some homework is pointless — copying notes or colouring in a poster teaches me nothing. But projects where I have to find things out for myself are different; I've learned more from those than from some lessons. It's not the amount that matters, it's whether it makes you think.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which person refers to research that shows different results for different age groups?
parts.working: C: moderate homework helps secondary students; little evidence for young children.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which person values homework as a way of checking understanding?
parts.working: A: homework shows who has really understood.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which person is concerned about the effect of homework on a child's free time?
parts.working: B: hasn't played outside in months.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which person distinguishes between useful and useless tasks?
parts.working: D: copying notes pointless; research projects valuable.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which person prefers a smaller quantity of better tasks?
parts.working: A: ten well-chosen rather than forty repetitive. D also says quality matters but does not compare quantities.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which person suggests better coordination is needed?
parts.working: B: schools need to talk to each other about how much they set.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Which person says there is a limit beyond which homework stops helping?
parts.working: C: beyond a certain point the benefit disappears.

parts.label: h
parts.text: Which person compares homework favourably with some classroom teaching?
parts.working: D: learned more from projects than some lessons.

parts.label: i
parts.text: Which person describes the total amount of study a child does outside school?
parts.working: B: three hours a night plus weekend tuition.

practice.subtopic: Matching to four texts or sections (A–D)
practice.stem:
Read what four people say about taking a break from their phones, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once.

Switching off

A  Amna, 18
I deleted the social media apps for a month, mainly to prove to myself that I could. I expected to be bored, but I actually read three novels. The people I missed most were the ones I had been ignoring in person all along.

B  Joseph, 35
My phone is now in a drawer by eight o'clock every evening. I still check my emails, but I stopped answering them at night. My family has noticed the difference, though I suspect my colleagues have not forgiven me yet.

C  Hira, 24
I tried a digital detox at a mountain retreat. The rules were strict, and there was no signal anyway. Honestly, I found the silence unsettling at first. By the third day, though, I was sleeping better than I have in years.

D  Dev, 16
Taking a break sounds nice, but it isn't realistic when all my homework is online. I mostly just move my screen time to a different app. The real problem is that nobody has told me what I'm supposed to do instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which person suggests that a break from technology improved their relationships with others?
parts.working: A: people I missed most were the ones I had been ignoring in person.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which person implies that their motive for stopping was partly to test their own self-discipline?
parts.working: A: to prove to myself that I could.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which person implies that a change in habit has caused friction at work?
parts.working: B: colleagues have not forgiven me; stopped answering at night.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which person suggests the first part of a break felt uncomfortable?
parts.working: C: found the silence unsettling at first.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which person suggests that the rules of a retreat limited them?
parts.working: C: rules were strict and there was no signal.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which person suggests that their sleep improved after a break?
parts.working: C: sleeping better than in years.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Which person suggests that a break is impractical because of schoolwork?
parts.working: D: not realistic when all my homework is online.

parts.label: h
parts.text: Which person implies that the break did not reduce their overall screen use?
parts.working: D: move my screen time to a different app.

parts.label: i
parts.text: Which person says the main problem is a lack of guidance on what to do instead?
parts.working: D: nobody has told me what I'm supposed to do instead.

practice.subtopic: Matching to four texts or sections (A–D)
practice.stem:
Read what four people say about a new school uniform rule, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once.

What to wear

A  Principal Hamid
The new uniform policy is a sensible step. Families have told us that the old rules were confusing, and the revised dress code will make mornings quicker for everyone. We will review its impact at the end of the year.

B  Parent, Mrs Iqbal
I welcome a uniform, but the price of the official blazer is out of reach for many families. The school should either reduce the cost or accept second-hand items, because children should not feel excluded.

C  Student, Usman
Wearing the same clothes every day feels like a punishment. Nobody asked us for our opinion. Some of my friends will find a way around the rules, which will only create more arguments with teachers.

D  Teacher, Ms Saba
Dress codes make it easier to focus on learning rather than appearance. However, I think the policy should have been introduced gradually. Sudden change tends to produce resentment, and that is what I am seeing in my classes this week.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which person suggests that the rules had been unclear before?
parts.working: A: old rules were confusing.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which person implies that the rule might cause conflict rather than solve problems?

parts.label: d

parts.working: B: price out of reach for many families.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which person suggests a way to make the policy fairer by accepting cheaper clothing?
parts.working: B: accept second-hand items.

parts.label: f

parts.working: D: should have been introduced gradually.

parts.label: g

practice.subtopic: Matching to four texts or sections (A–D)
practice.stem:
Read what four people say about visiting a science museum, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once.

Was it worth it?

A  Rafay, 14
The planetarium was the best part. I didn't expect to be so moved by the stars on the ceiling, and I'd happily go back tomorrow. The rest of the museum was packed with children, though, so it was hard to see any of the exhibits properly.

B  Nadia, 52
I took my grandchildren, and I was surprised by how much I enjoyed the hands-on displays. The staff were patient with my questions. The only disappointment was the café, which charged more than the cinema next door.

C  Stefan, 33
Honestly, the museum felt more like a shop than a place of learning. The most interesting objects were behind glass with tiny labels. I'd have preferred fewer gadgets and more real explanations of how things work.

D  Mariam, 20
The exhibition on early computing was excellent. I spent most of the afternoon reading the notes beside each machine. I would only suggest that the museum adds guided tours, because the displays are so detailed that it is easy to miss the best parts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which person says that a visit made them want to return to a particular experience?
parts.working: A: I'd happily go back tomorrow.

parts.label: b

parts.working: A: packed with children; hard to see the exhibits.

parts.label: c

parts.working: B: staff were patient with my questions.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which person implies that spending on food felt unreasonable?
parts.working: B: café charged more than the cinema next door.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which person suggests that the museum prioritises selling rather than teaching?
parts.working: C: felt more like a shop than a place of learning.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which person prefers the content to be explained in more depth?
parts.working: C: more real explanations of how things work.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Which person suggests that the visitor spent a long time in one area?
parts.working: D: spent most of the afternoon reading notes.

parts.label: h
parts.text: Which person suggests that a service would help visitors make the most of the displays?
parts.working: D: guided tours.

parts.label: i
parts.text: Which person says they were surprised by how much they liked something?
parts.working: B: surprised by how much I enjoyed hands-on displays.

practice.subtopic: Matching to four texts or sections (A–D)
practice.stem:
Read what four people say about keeping pets, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once.

Pets and responsibility

A  Kiran, 27
A dog is a commitment that lasts fifteen years. People buy puppies at Eid or on a whim, then give them away when the novelty fades. I would never let my dog go, but I think more people should read about the cost before they start.

B  Mrs Parveen, 67
My cat keeps me company since my husband passed away. The vet bills are high, and I do worry about who will look after her if I am admitted to hospital one day. Still, she has given me a reason to get up each morning.

C  Ellis, 40
We adopted a rescue rabbit and then realised it needed a bigger enclosure than the flat allowed. The landlord was unhappy, and the rabbit was unhappy too. We now keep it in a garden shed, which is far from ideal.

D  Zara, 12
My hamster is brilliant, but I think it's cruel to keep one in a small cage. It only runs when it's out. My parents say the cage is big enough, but I have seen the wheel, and it's too small for a running hamster.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which person suggests that some owners do not consider long-term costs?
parts.working: A: people buy puppies on a whim and give them away.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which person implies that they feel responsible for the future of their pet?
parts.working: B: who will look after her if I am admitted to hospital.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which person suggests that a pet has improved their emotional wellbeing?
parts.working: B: she has given me a reason to get up each morning; keeps me company.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which person implies that the pet did not suit the home they had?
parts.working: C: enclosure bigger than the flat allowed.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which person implies that a living arrangement was accepted as a compromise?
parts.working: C: garden shed, far from ideal.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which person implies that a parent is not aware of a problem?
parts.working: D: parents say the cage is big enough, but I have seen the wheel.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Which person suggests that an animal's behaviour is linked to the space it has?
parts.working: D: only runs when it's out; wheel too small.

parts.label: h
parts.text: Which person suggests that a pet should be kept for life?
parts.working: A: a commitment that lasts fifteen years; I would never let my dog go.

parts.label: i
parts.text: Which person describes a practical problem in finding housing that suits a pet?
parts.working: C: landlord unhappy; enclosure bigger than the flat allowed.

practice.subtopic: Matching to four texts or sections (A–D)
practice.stem:
Read what four people say about learning a musical instrument, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once.

Practice makes perfect?

A  Pooja, 30
I took up the violin at thirty because I had always envied my friends who could play. The first year was painful: I could only produce squeaks. Now I play in an amateur orchestra, and my teacher says I'm finally ready to perform a solo.

B  Victor, 58
I bought a keyboard during lockdown and taught myself from videos. I could never read music, so I learned to play by ear. My family says I sound best when I stop trying to be perfect, and I think they are right.

C  Anika, 11
I hate practising. My piano teacher says that ten minutes a day is enough, but I always forget. The only time I really enjoy the piano is when my grandmother comes to visit and asks me to play her favourite song.

D  Ali, 22
I studied classical guitar for six years, but I stopped when I realised that I didn't want to be a professional. I still pick up the guitar, though now I play only the songs I like, without any technique at all, and I'm happier for it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which person suggests that a long-held wish motivated them to begin learning?
parts.working: A: always envied my friends who could play.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which person says that progress was initially discouraging?
parts.working: A: the first year was painful; squeaks.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which person implies that they have no formal training in reading music?
parts.working: B: could never read music; learned by ear.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which person says that a relaxed attitude helped them to enjoy playing?
parts.working: B: sound best when I stop trying to be perfect.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which person suggests that their practice routine is not a priority?
parts.working: C: hate practising; always forget.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which person suggests that a family member encourages their playing?
parts.working: C: grandmother asks me to play her favourite song.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Which person suggests that they decided against pursuing music as a job?
parts.working: D: didn't want to be a professional.

parts.label: h
parts.text: Which person says they now choose only music they like?
parts.working: D: play only the songs I like.

parts.label: i
parts.text: Which person suggests that they are now able to perform in public?
parts.working: A: an amateur orchestra; ready to perform a solo.

practice.subtopic: Matching to four texts or sections (A–D)
practice.stem:
Read what four people say about ways of reducing waste at home, and then answer the questions. For each question, write the correct letter A, B, C or D. Each letter may be used more than once.

Less rubbish, more thought

A  Salman, 46
We stopped buying bottled water years ago and now carry a steel flask to work. It's a small change, but my colleagues have started doing it too. I find that people are more willing to change when they see someone doing it at ease.

B  Ruth, 38
I compost my kitchen scraps and give the result to the allotment next door. The compost bin attracts flies in summer, which my husband complains about, but our vegetables have never been better. It's a trade-off I accept.

C  Tanya, 19
I keep buying new clothes, mostly because they are cheap. I know I should stop, and I feel guilty every time I open a delivery box. Realistically, I need to find a better reason than guilt to change my habits.

D  Imran, 33
Recycling is pointless if the council just sends everything to landfill. I sort my rubbish every week, but I'm not convinced it makes any difference. Until the government takes it seriously, individual effort feels a little hopeless.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which person suggests that their example encouraged others to change?
parts.working: A: my colleagues have started doing it too.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which person implies that some people are more likely to change if the change looks effortless?
parts.working: A: when they see someone doing it at ease.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which person accepts a drawback of their method for a benefit?
parts.working: B: a trade-off I accept (flies in summer, better vegetables).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which person suggests that a family member is not happy with a home activity?
parts.working: B: my husband complains about flies.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Which person admits to a habit they know they should stop?
parts.working: C: keep buying new clothes; I know I should stop.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Which person suggests that a stronger motive than guilt is needed?
parts.working: C: find a better reason than guilt to change.

parts.label: g
parts.text: Which person suggests that their efforts seem pointless without action from authorities?
parts.working: D: individual effort feels hopeless until government acts.

parts.label: h
parts.text: Which person says that the recycling they do may not lead to a real outcome?
parts.working: D: not convinced it makes any difference.

parts.label: i
parts.text: Which person says that they continue to sort rubbish weekly?
parts.working: D: I sort my rubbish every week.

When this gas reaches the surface of your eyes, it irritates them, and your eyes produce tears to wash it away. So what can you do? Chilling the onion in the fridge for half an hour helps, because the gas is released more slowly when it's cold. And using a sharp knife is better than a blunt one, which crushes more cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Why do our eyes produce tears when we cut onions?
parts.answer: to wash away the gas / because the gas irritates them

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why is a sharp knife better than a blunt one?
parts.answer: a blunt knife crushes more cells (releasing more gas)

Good afternoon. I'd like to talk about one of the most valuable but least appreciated habitats on Earth: mangrove forests. Mangroves are trees that grow in salty water along tropical coasts. Pakistan has large mangrove forests in the Indus delta, south of Karachi.
Mangroves are remarkable because most plants die in salt water. Mangroves survive partly by getting rid of salt through their leaves, and their roots are specially adapted. Some species have roots that stick up out of the mud like pencils. These roots, called pneumatophores, allow the tree to take in air, because the mud itself contains very little oxygen.
Why do mangroves matter? Firstly, they protect the coast. Their tangled roots slow down waves and storm surges, so villages behind them suffer less damage during cyclones. Thirdly, and this is something many people don't realise, mangroves store a huge amount of carbon, much of it in the mud beneath them rather than in the trees themselves.
In the past, mangroves were cut down for firewood and to make space for shrimp farms. But the good news is that replanting projects in Sindh have been very successful, and the area of mangrove forest there has grown in recent years.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Hello. Today I want to talk about something most young people never think about until it's too late: your hearing. Inside your inner ear are thousands of tiny hair cells that turn sound vibrations into signals for the brain. Once these cells are damaged, they don't grow back, so hearing loss caused by noise is permanent.
Sound is measured in decibels. Normal conversation is about sixty decibels. Heavy city traffic is around eighty-five, and that's roughly the level at which damage can begin if you're exposed for long periods. A loud concert can reach over a hundred.
The biggest risk for teenagers is personal music players. Many people turn the volume up to block out traffic noise on buses or trains. A useful rule is the sixty–sixty rule: listen at no more than sixty per cent of maximum volume, for no more than sixty minutes at a time.
Warning signs include ringing in the ears, which doctors call tinnitus, or finding it hard to follow conversations in noisy places. If you notice these, see a doctor.
My advice is simple: choose noise-cancelling headphones, which reduce background noise so you don't need to turn the music up, and carry foam earplugs if you go to concerts or weddings with loud music. They're cheap and they really work.

A solar panel is made of many small cells, usually made from silicon. When sunlight hits a cell, it knocks tiny particles called electrons loose, and this flow of electrons is an electric current. The electricity produced is direct current, but our homes use alternating current, so every system needs a device called an inverter to convert it.
The direction a panel faces matters a lot. In Pakistan, panels should face south and be tilted at roughly the same angle as the local latitude. Shade is a big enemy: even a shadow from a water tank on part of one panel can reduce the output of the whole row.

You will hear a talk by a psychologist about how memory works and how students can revise more effectively. Complete the notes. Write no more than three words or a number in each gap.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Most students revise in the same way: they read their notes again and again and highlight the important parts in bright colours. Unfortunately, research suggests that this is one of the least effective ways to learn. It makes material feel familiar, which tricks us into thinking we know it, but familiarity is not the same as being able to recall it in an exam.
So what works better? The technique with the strongest evidence is called retrieval practice. Instead of re-reading, you close the book and try to bring the information back from memory — for example, by testing yourself with flashcards or writing down everything you can remember about a topic. Every time you successfully recall something, the memory becomes stronger.
The second technique is spacing. Rather than revising a topic for three hours in one day, it's far better to study it for one hour on three separate days. The forgetting that happens between sessions actually helps, because the brain has to work harder to retrieve the information.
A third approach is called interleaving: mixing different types of problems in one session, rather than practising the same type again and again. It feels harder and more frustrating, which is why students tend to avoid it, but it improves your ability to choose the right method in an exam.
Finally, never underestimate sleep. During sleep, the brain transfers new memories into long-term storage. Staying up all night before an exam is about the worst thing you can do.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
When people think of plastic pollution, they usually picture bottles and bags floating on the surface of the sea. But what worries scientists most is the plastic you can't see. Over time, sunlight and waves break larger items into smaller and smaller fragments. Pieces less than five millimetres across are called microplastics, and they've now been found everywhere, from Arctic ice to the deepest ocean trenches.
Microplastics don't only come from broken-down rubbish. A surprising amount comes from synthetic clothes: every time polyester or nylon clothing goes through a washing machine, it releases thousands of tiny fibres that pass through water treatment plants and into rivers. Car tyres are another major source, as they wear down on roads and the dust is washed into drains.
Why does this matter? Small sea creatures such as plankton mistake microplastics for food. These are eaten by fish, which in turn are eaten by larger animals, including humans. Scientists are still investigating the effects on human health, so we should be careful not to exaggerate, but microplastics have been found in seafood and even in drinking water.
Some solutions are simple. Filters fitted to washing machines can catch many of the fibres. Choosing natural fabrics like cotton helps, too. But the most effective step is to stop plastic entering the environment in the first place — that means reducing single-use packaging, not just recycling it.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Long before air conditioning was invented, people living in hot, dry regions found clever ways to keep their homes cool. Many of these ideas are being rediscovered by architects today, as electricity prices rise and summers get hotter.
One of the most famous examples is the windcatcher, a tall tower on the roof with openings facing the wind. In parts of Sindh, houses traditionally had a similar structure called a 'mangh', which caught the cool evening breeze and directed it down into the rooms below. In Iran, windcatchers were sometimes combined with underground water channels, which cooled the air even further before it entered the house.
Another technique is thermal mass. Thick walls made of stone or mud brick absorb heat slowly during the day, so the inside stays cool. At night, when the air outside is cooler, the walls release the heat they have stored.
Courtyards also play an important role. A courtyard with trees and a small fountain creates a pocket of cooler air, because water absorbs heat as it evaporates. The rooms around the courtyard draw on this cool air.
Finally, there's the jali, a carved stone or wooden screen with small holes. It lets air through while blocking direct sunlight, and also provides privacy. Modern buildings in Lahore and Karachi are starting to use concrete versions of the jali on their outside walls.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
We're often told that breakfast is the most important meal of the day. The truth is a little more complicated, and the research is not as clear-cut as advertisements suggest. What does seem clear is that what you eat matters more than simply whether you eat.
Let's start with energy. Your brain runs mainly on glucose, a type of sugar. Foods such as sugary cereals or white bread release glucose very quickly. You feel alert for a short time, but within a couple of hours your blood sugar falls, and many people feel tired and find it hard to concentrate. This is sometimes called a 'sugar crash'.
A better choice is food that releases energy slowly. Whole grains, such as oats or wholemeal bread, take longer to digest. Adding protein, like eggs, yoghurt or lentils, also slows digestion and keeps you feeling full until lunchtime. So a traditional breakfast of an egg and a wholemeal roti is actually an excellent choice.
Some studies of schoolchildren have found that those who eat a balanced breakfast perform better in memory tasks during the morning. However, it's worth noting that children who eat breakfast may also differ in other ways — for example, they may sleep more regularly — so we can't be sure breakfast is the only cause.
Finally, don't forget drinking water. Even mild dehydration can reduce concentration, and many students arrive at school without having drunk anything.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Mars has fascinated people for centuries, partly because of its colour. Its red appearance comes from iron oxide — basically rust — in the dust that covers its surface.
Mars is smaller than Earth, roughly half its diameter, and its gravity is only about thirty-eight per cent of Earth's, so you could jump much higher there. A day on Mars is only slightly longer than ours, about twenty-four hours and forty minutes, but a year lasts almost twice as long, because Mars is further from the Sun.
The atmosphere is very thin and made mostly of carbon dioxide. It cannot trap much heat, so temperatures can drop far below freezing at night, even near the equator. Mars also has the largest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons, which is about two and a half times the height of Mount Everest.
Scientists are especially interested in whether there was ever life on Mars. Today, the surface is dry, but rovers have found evidence of ancient river valleys and lake beds, which shows that liquid water once flowed there. Water ice still exists at the poles and beneath the surface.
Sending humans to Mars remains extremely difficult. The journey would take around seven months each way, and astronauts would be exposed to dangerous radiation, because Mars has no global magnetic field to protect its surface.

My name is Faisal and I've been climbing for fifteen years. Today I want to tell you about my first big expedition, to a mountain in the Karakoram about six thousand metres high. I was twenty-two and, looking back, far too confident.
We spent the first week walking to base camp. Most people think the climbing is the hardest part, but for me it was the altitude. Above four thousand metres I got terrible headaches and couldn't sleep. Our guide, a man from Hushe called Ibrahim, made us stop for two days so our bodies could adjust.
The weather was the next problem. We had planned to reach the summit on the tenth day, but a storm kept us in our tents for three days. We ran short of food and had to share one packet of noodles between four people.
In the end we didn't reach the top. About three hundred metres below the summit, Ibrahim decided the snow was too unstable and turned us back. I was furious at the time, but two days later we heard that the slope had collapsed in an avalanche.
That climb taught me the most important rule in the mountains: the summit is optional, but coming home is not. I've reached many summits since, but I still think of that failed climb as my most important one.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
In parts of East Africa, there is a remarkable partnership between humans and a wild bird called the greater honeyguide. As the name suggests, the bird leads people to bees' nests hidden in trees.
The honeyguide can find nests easily, but it can't break into them because of the bees' stings. Humans, on the other hand, can use fire and axes to open the nest. After the honey hunters take the honey, the bird eats the wax that is left behind. Interestingly, it's the wax the bird wants, not the honey.
What fascinated our research team was how the two species communicate. The Yao people of Mozambique use a special call — a loud trill followed by a grunt — to tell honeyguides they're ready to follow. We played recordings of this call and of other sounds, and found the birds were far more likely to guide people who used the traditional call.
In Tanzania, the Hadza people use a different, whistled call. So, just as human languages vary from place to place, the signals used with the birds seem to vary too. We suspect young birds learn the local call by experience.
Sadly, this partnership is disappearing in some areas, as people buy sugar instead of collecting wild honey. Where people stop honey hunting, the birds stop guiding.

When I started studying computer science, I never imagined I'd design apps for people with disabilities. It happened by accident. My younger brother, Hamza, is blind, and when he got his first smartphone, I saw how frustrating many apps were for him. Buttons had no labels, so his screen reader just said 'button, button, button'.
My first project was a simple app that reads bus numbers aloud as buses approach a stop, using the phone's camera. Hamza tested it at every stage. He was a very honest critic — he once told me a version was 'completely useless', which hurt, but he was right.
Many developers think accessible design is expensive and only helps a small number of people. Actually, it benefits everyone. Think of captions on videos: they were designed for deaf people, but millions of people use them to watch videos quietly on buses.
The hardest part of my work isn't the technology; it's persuading companies to care. Often they only make changes after a complaint, or because the law requires it.
My advice to young developers is this: don't design for people with disabilities, design with them. Invite them into the process from the beginning, not just at the end to test something that's already finished.

practice.stem:
You will hear a talk by a journalist about how to spot false news online. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Every day, millions of people share stories online without checking whether they're true. Some false stories are harmless, but others can cause real damage — for example, rumours about medicines during a health emergency.
The first thing I tell students is to notice their own feelings. False stories are often designed to make you angry or frightened, because emotional people share things quickly without thinking. So if a headline makes you furious, that's exactly the moment to slow down.
Secondly, look at the source. Is it a news organisation you recognise? Be careful: some fake websites copy the logo of real newspapers and change just one letter in the web address.
Thirdly, check the date. A surprising number of 'news' stories are actually years old and are shared again as if they were happening today. Photos are a particular problem. A picture of flooding from one country may be shared as if it shows a different country. You can use a reverse image search to find where a photo first appeared.
Finally, don't assume something is true just because lots of people have shared it, or because a friend sent it. Our friends are often the least careful sources of all, because we trust them. If you're not sure, the simplest rule is: don't share.

My name is Haider and I paint trucks — not with ordinary paint, but in the style that has made Pakistani trucks famous around the world. I learned from my father, who worked in a truck-art workshop in Karachi for forty years.
A fully decorated truck can take up to two months to finish. We cover it with flowers, peacocks, poetry and portraits, and fix shining metal pieces and chains to the bumpers. Truck owners often spend more on decoration than they spend on the engine. For many drivers, who spend weeks away from home, the truck is like a second house, so they want it to be beautiful.

Fifteen years ago, I worried this art might die out, because young people weren't interested in learning. Ironically, it was foreigners who saved it. Designers from Europe began asking us to decorate everything from cups to cars, and suddenly truck art became fashionable in Pakistan too.
Now I teach workshops at an art college. My students are mostly university graduates, which would have amazed my father.

You will hear a talk by a nurse about working in a hospital at night. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
I've worked night shifts in a children's hospital in Karachi for eight years. My shift starts at eight in the evening and finishes at eight the next morning. People imagine nights are quiet, but in a children's ward they rarely are. Children often feel more frightened in the dark, so a lot of my work is simply comforting them.
The first thing I do each evening is the handover, when the day nurses tell us about every patient. It's the most important part of the shift, because if information is missed, mistakes can happen.
The hardest time is between three and five in the morning. That's when I feel most tired, and it's also, strangely, when many children's conditions change. I drink a lot of water rather than tea, because too much caffeine makes it hard to sleep when I get home.
Sleeping in the day was difficult at first. I now use thick curtains and switch my phone off, and my family knows not to disturb me before two o'clock.
What I love about nights is the teamwork. With fewer staff, doctors and nurses rely on each other completely. And there is no better feeling than watching the sun rise after helping a sick child through a difficult night.

You will hear a university lecturer speaking about the history of coffee in the Middle East. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Good afternoon. Coffee's origins are usually traced to the highlands of Ethiopia, but the first documented coffee houses appeared in Yemen during the fifteenth century. Yemeni traders grew coffee on terraced hillsides and shipped it through the port of Mocha, which gave its name to a famous type of coffee.
Coffee houses soon became places for conversation, music and games. Some rulers were suspicious of them, because people discussed politics there. In several cities, authorities briefly banned coffee, but the bans never lasted for long.
By the seventeenth century, coffee had reached Istanbul, where it became extremely popular. The Ottomans developed a method of preparing it that is still used today, with very finely ground beans and a small copper pot.
So coffee is not only a drink, but also a social institution, and the coffee house is perhaps its most important legacy.

practice.stem:
You will hear a talk by an economist about why people buy things they do not need. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Economists used to assume that people make rational decisions: we compare prices, think about what we need, and choose the best option. But research in behavioural economics shows that our choices are influenced by all sorts of hidden factors.
Take 'anchoring'. If a jacket is labelled 'was 10,000 rupees, now 6,000', we feel we're getting a bargain, even if we'd never have paid 10,000 in the first place. The first number acts as an anchor, and everything is judged against it.
Another trick is the decoy. A café might sell a small coffee for 300 rupees, a large for 500, and a medium for 480. Hardly anyone buys the medium, but it isn't meant to be bought; its job is to make the large look like excellent value.
Then there's what we call loss aversion. People feel the pain of losing something about twice as strongly as the pleasure of gaining the same thing. That's why 'free trials' are so effective. Once we have something, giving it up feels like a loss, so many people keep paying.
I'm not saying all shopping is foolish. But understanding these techniques gives you power. Before buying, ask yourself: would I want this if there were no sale sign, no countdown clock, no 'only three left' message? If the answer is no, you probably don't need it.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
For more than a century, people have believed that your position in the family shapes your personality. Firstborn children are said to be responsible and ambitious, middle children are supposed to be peacemakers, and the youngest are often described as charming but spoiled.
These ideas are so widespread that many parents treat them as facts. However, when researchers began studying very large groups — in one case, data from over twenty thousand people in three countries — they found that birth order had almost no effect on personality traits such as confidence or kindness.
Why did earlier studies find differences? Partly because they compared siblings at the same moment. A twelve-year-old naturally seems more responsible than her eight-year-old brother, but that's because she's older, not because she was born first.
There is one area where a small effect does seem to exist: firstborns score very slightly higher, on average, in intelligence tests. One explanation is that eldest children often explain things to younger siblings, which strengthens their own understanding. But the difference is tiny, and it tells you nothing about any particular child.
So why do the myths survive? I think it's because they make good stories. We notice examples that fit our expectations and forget the ones that don't. My advice to parents is to see each child as an individual, not as a position in the family.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
After the 2005 earthquake in northern Pakistan, which destroyed hundreds of thousands of homes, I joined a team helping villagers rebuild. One thing I learned quickly is that earthquakes themselves rarely kill people. It's collapsing buildings that do.
Many houses in the mountains were built of heavy stone held together with mud. These walls are strong when pushed straight down, but when the ground shakes from side to side, they crack and fall apart. Flat concrete roofs made things worse, because their great weight crushed the people underneath.
Interestingly, some old traditional houses survived better than modern ones. In parts of Kashmir, builders had used a method in which horizontal wooden beams were laid into the stone walls every metre or so. The wood holds the stones together and allows the building to bend slightly instead of breaking.
Our team encouraged a mix of old and new ideas: walls with wooden or steel bands, lighter roofs made of metal sheets, and smaller windows placed away from corners, because corners are where cracks usually begin.
The hardest part wasn't the engineering. Families wanted to rebuild quickly, before winter, and some saw safety features as unnecessary costs. We found that the most effective way to persuade them was not lectures but demonstrations, where we shook small model houses on a moving table so people could see the difference with their own eyes.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Today it's hard to imagine Pakistan without chai. It's served at every office, every wedding, every roadside stop. But tea drinking became widespread here surprisingly recently — mainly in the twentieth century.
The British began growing tea in Assam in the nineteenth century, but almost all of it was sent to Britain. Local people, on the whole, didn't drink it. In fact, in the early twentieth century, the tea industry ran large advertising campaigns to persuade South Asians to start. Salesmen travelled to railway stations and factories, showing people how to make tea and handing out free cups.
The campaigns recommended tea made the British way, with just a little milk and sugar. But people adapted it to their own tastes. They boiled the leaves together with lots of milk, sugar and sometimes spices such as cardamom and ginger. The result was the strong, sweet chai we know today. Ironically, some officials disapproved of this, because using less tea per cup meant fewer sales.
In the north, a quite different tradition already existed. In Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, people drank green tea, often with salt, which had arrived along trade routes from Central Asia and China centuries before the British.
So next time you drink a cup of chai, remember that it's a product of colonial business, clever marketing and local creativity all mixed together.

You will hear an interview with Mahnoor Ali, a young woman who runs a bakery in Karachi. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Mahnoor, you opened your bakery at just twenty-two. How did it start?
Mahnoor: Honestly, by accident. I was studying accounting, and I baked cakes for friends' birthdays as a hobby. Then a friend posted a photo of one of my cakes online, and suddenly strangers were messaging me with orders. Within six months I was baking more than I was studying!
Interviewer: What was the hardest part of starting a business?
Mahnoor: People expect me to say money, but my family lent me enough to rent a small kitchen. Finding good staff wasn't easy either, but the real challenge was time. I was getting up at four every morning and finishing at ten at night. I didn't see my friends for months.
Interviewer: What's your best-selling product?
Mahnoor: Everyone assumes it's the chocolate cake, because that's what made me famous. But actually it's our cardamom biscuits. Office workers buy them by the box to have with their tea.
Interviewer: And what's next for you?
Mahnoor: I've been asked to open a second shop in Lahore, but I'm not ready for that. Instead, I want to start baking classes for teenagers on Saturday mornings. I think everyone should know how to bake bread.

parts.text:
How did Mahnoor's business begin?
A She sold cakes to her classmates.
B A friend shared a picture of her cake online.
C She studied baking at college.

parts.working: A friend posted a photo online and strangers started ordering. She studied accounting, not baking; she baked for friends' birthdays, not to sell to classmates.

parts.label: b
parts.text:

You will hear an interview with Asad Mir, a wildlife photographer who photographs snow leopards in northern Pakistan. For each question, choose the correct answer, A, B or C.

Transcript (read it aloud, or read it silently)
Interviewer: Asad, snow leopards are famously hard to see. How long did it take you to photograph one?
Asad: Three winters! I spent weeks in the mountains of Chitral and saw footprints and droppings, but never the animal. The first time I actually saw one, it was across a valley, too far away for a good photo.
Interviewer: So how did you finally get your pictures?
Asad: Local herders helped me most. They know exactly which paths the leopards use. I also set up camera traps – cameras that take a photo automatically when an animal walks past. Most of my best pictures come from those, not from me holding the camera.
Interviewer: Aren't the herders angry with snow leopards for killing their goats?
Asad: They used to be. But now there's an insurance scheme: if a leopard kills an animal, the family receives money. So herders are much less likely to harm the leopards.
Interviewer: What do you most want people to feel when they see your photos?
Asad: Not just that the animals are beautiful. I want them to realise that leopards and people can share the mountains.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What happened the first time Asad saw a snow leopard?
A It was too far away to photograph well.
B It ran away when it heard him.
C He took his best photograph.
parts.answer: A It was too far away to photograph well.
parts.working: It was across a valley, too far for a good photo.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Where do most of Asad's best photos come from?
A photos he took himself
B photos taken by herders
C camera traps
parts.working: 'Most of my best pictures come from those [camera traps], not from me holding the camera.' Herders show paths but don't take the photos.

parts.label: c
parts.text:

B They earn money from tourists.
C They are paid if a leopard kills an animal.
parts.answer: C They are paid if a leopard kills an animal.
parts.working: The insurance scheme gives families money.

Interviewer: How did people react?

Interviewer: What's the most difficult thing about the job?
Shaista: The heat in summer is tiring, and the traffic is terrible, but the worst thing is finding a place to rest. There are very few places in the city where a woman driver can stop, have a cup of tea and use a clean bathroom.
Interviewer: What would you say to other women?
Shaista: If you need to work, don't let anyone tell you that a job is only for men.

Zeeshan: Some species are coming in smaller numbers, mainly because hunters still shoot them on their journey, even though it's illegal. But ducks have increased since the lake was cleaned up two years ago.

Zeeshan: Between December and February, early in the morning. Bring warm clothes and, if you can, binoculars. Please don't bring bread to feed the birds – it isn't good for them.

Mrs Javed: Older students, from Class 9, spend twenty minutes twice a week reading with younger children from Class 3. They choose books together and talk about the stories.
Interviewer: Why did you start it?

Interviewer: How is a forecast prepared?
Nida: We use information from satellites, weather balloons and stations all over the country. Computers turn this into predictions, but forecasters still check them, because the computer can make mistakes, especially in the mountains.

Nida: Thunderstorms. They can form very quickly over a small area, so one town gets heavy rain and the next stays dry.
